docs.title: Mujou
docs.text:
Asynchronous Distributed Deep Learning Library for Continuous Learning

Image: a new work based on Yoichi Ochiai's Liquid Universe.

Mujou is a deep learning framework that keeps inferring and learning at the same time. You write nodes in PyTorch code and run a network that connects them.

Early development

Mujou is in an early stage of development. The API may change without notice.

docs.title: 🌱 A network that keeps learning
docs.text:
Conventional machine learning trains a model, then freezes its weights for inference. A Mujou network takes input and produces output for as long as it runs, and keeps learning at the same time.

There is no mode to switch between training and inference, and there are no epochs.

The name comes from 無常 (mujō, impermanence: nothing stays the same), as in the Buddhist phrase 諸行無常. Mujou is a framework for machines that keep learning from a stream and keep changing. It targets uses that learn while they act, such as real-time processing and robotics.

The program below is such a network: a chain of PC-ALM nodes, three of them learning, that learns a regression from a stream of batches. Each batch is predicted before the nodes learn from it, while the nodes keep running.

SHOWN = 0.032  # seconds of the run's timer each batch is shown
# tau.h sets how fast the activities relax (and the period of the nodes, h / 4),
# and the weights learn once per batch, by SGD at the rate SHOWN / theta = 0.3.
tau = pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=8e-3, theta=SHOWN / 0.3)
torch.manual_seed(0)  # the initial weights, before the run
net = pc.Chain(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 64), nn.Tanh()),
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh()),
    nn.Linear(64, 1),
    x=TensorSpec((B, 2)),
    y=TensorSpec((B, 1)),
    batch=B,
    loss=pc.MSELoss(B),  # the loss of each sample, (B,)
    tau=tau,
    learn_interval=0.75 * SHOWN,  # learn once, 3/4 of the way through each batch
)

torch.set_num_threads(1)
g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)
every = torch.ones(B, dtype=torch.bool)  # every sample has a target
losses: list[float] = []
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    for i in range(300):
        x = 2 * torch.rand(B, 2, generator=g) - 1
        y = torch.sin(2 * x[:, :1]) * torch.cos(x[:, 1:])
        p = pc.show(run, net, pc.Sample(x=x, y=y, mask=every), seconds=SHOWN)
        losses.append(nn.functional.mse_loss(p["y_hat"], y).item())  # before learning
        if i == 0 or (i + 1) % 50 == 0:
            recent = losses[-50:]
            mean = sum(recent) / len(recent)
            print(
                f"batch {i + 1:3d}: loss {mean:.4f} (the mean of the last {len(recent)})"
            )
    # The state of a node, by its path: input, layer0, layer1, output.
    lam = run.state_dict()["nodes"]["layer0"]["state"]["lam"]
print(f"the mean |lam| of layer0 (its credit) at the end: {lam.abs().mean():.2e}")

docs.title: ✨ Features
docs.text:
• 🔄 Inference and learning at once: no training mode, no inference mode, no epochs
  • 🧩 Nodes in PyTorch: write each node in ordinary PyTorch code, run synchronously inside the node
  • ⚡ Asynchronous nodes: each node updates on its own schedule and never waits for another
  • ⏱️ Continuous time: nodes update in proportion to dt, the time that really passed
  • 🧠 Any update rule: backpropagation inside a node, PC-ALM across nodes, or a rule of your own
  • 💾 State without stopping: take the state of a running network and resume from it later
  • 🧪 Deterministic tests: a virtual timer and manual updates for testing nodes

docs.title: ⚙️ How it runs
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    H["Host (your program)"] -->|"writes inputs"| A["Node A"]
    A -->|"latest value"| B["Node B"]
    B -->|"reads outputs"| H

Each node repeats its update on its own schedule and never waits for another node; it reads the latest value its neighbor sent.

The host (the program that runs the network) writes inputs to the running network and reads its outputs.

docs.title: 🧠 How Mujou Works
docs.text:
This page explains the nine ideas you need to use Mujou, in the order you meet them, and ends with the rules a node keeps. The Tutorial puts them to work.

flowchart TB
    H["Host (the Python code that drives the network)"]
    subgraph N["Network"]
        direction LR
        A["Node A"] <-->|Channel| B["Node B"] <-->|Channel| C["Node C"]
    end
    T["The run's timer"]
    H -->|"through the Run that mujou.run(net) returns: write inputs, read outputs, take the state"| N
    T -.->|"time and dt"| N

docs.title: 1. Nodes
docs.text:
A node is the unit of computation. You write it as a class that inherits from mujou.Node, and write one step of its work in on_update(dt). Mujou calls on_update over and over, so a node holds no loop of its own; it also calls other hooks, such as on_start and on_stop, whose order is in the API reference of Node.

Inside a node, ordinary PyTorch code runs synchronously, and records gradients as plain PyTorch does. Between nodes, everything is asynchronous: a node never waits for another, and talks to the others only through its ports. A node keeps its state in its own attributes.

The node class decides how much computation one node holds: one layer, several layers, or a whole model. The node boundaries are the asynchronous boundaries, so put layers that should compute (or learn by backpropagation) together in one node class.

docs.title: 2. Ports and channels
docs.text:
A port is a connection point of a node. connect joins two ports with one channel, and returns it.

  • A Port's recv() returns one value, so it receives from at most one peer. A Port that only sends reaches any number of peers
  • A MultiPort gathers peers of one kind. Its recv() returns a dict[Channel, value], in the order of connect, and the node decides how to combine them. Inputs of different roles (a prediction and an error, say) go to separate Ports
  • Connections may form cycles

Reading never waits and nothing queues: recv() returns the latest value the peer sent. Until the peer first sends, it returns the peer's initial value (zeros by default) with the time None. Every value carries the time it was sent, which tells whether it is new. More in Ports and Channels.

docs.title: 3. Message types (specs)
docs.text: A port declares what it sends and receives with a spec: TensorSpec(shape, dtype) for one tensor, or DictSpec for a TypedDict of tensors that travel together. The values are always torch.Tensor (or a dict of them). Two ports connect only when the spec each sends matches the spec the other receives, and send copies the value, detached from the computation graph.

docs.title: 4. Networks and paths
docs.text:
A Network is a container for building: you assign nodes to its attributes and connect their ports, as you give an nn.Module its submodules. Group(**named) is a network that only puts its children side by side under names. A network runs nothing itself; while running, the nodes inside it each run on their own.

A node's path is the attribute names from the root joined with dots, such as "body.l1". Paths are the keys of the state.

docs.title: 5. Runs
docs.text: mujou.run(root) checks the tree, starts every node, and returns a Run, the handle of the host (your program). The host writes inputs with write, reads outputs with read, wait_for and the like, and waits on run.timer. A root runs once: to run again, build new instances. After the run, the nodes' attributes are the host's to read.

docs.title: 6. Time
docs.text:
Each run has one time axis, its timer, used by every node and by the host: mujou.time.global_timer unless the run is given a Timer of its own. The host controls it through run.timer; a node only reads it, with self.timer.

dt is the time in seconds since the node's last update, on the run's timer. A node updates in proportion to dt, so that nodes updating at different and varying rates follow the same dynamics; a busy machine only makes dt longer. Each node updates once every period on average. Timeouts are the one exception: they are in real seconds. More in Time.

docs.title: 7. State
docs.text:
A node's state is collected automatically: its tensor attributes, its attributes with state_dict and load_state_dict (an nn.Module, say), and the state of its random generator. Other values that change while it runs (a counter, the time last seen, a list of tensors such as a replay buffer) join with register_state. The rules are in the API reference of Node.

run.state_dict() takes the state of the whole run at one time, without ending it: the nodes' states, the latest message on each channel and the time, in one plain dict. mujou.run(new_instance, state=tree) goes on from there, on a timer of its own that starts at the saved time. See Save and Resume.

docs.title: 8. Testing
docs.text: mujou.testing.run runs a tree on a virtual timer, deterministically: run.step(dt, *nodes) moves the time dt forward, then updates the nodes once each. See Test a Node.

docs.title: 9. Learning
docs.text:
An update rule is written inside the nodes: backpropagation inside one node, PC-ALM (the nodes of mujou.pc), or a rule of your own. Mujou builds no rule into nodes, ports or the scheduler. No computation graph crosses nodes, because a port sends a copy: what passes between nodes is messages, such as activities, errors and targets. See Learn in a Node, Learn with PC-ALM and Update Rules.

There is no training mode and no inference mode, and there are no epochs: a running network takes input, produces output and learns at the same time.

docs.title: Rules a node keeps
docs.text:
The other pages link here instead of repeating these.

  • Do not block with time.sleep. A node shares its worker thread with others, and a hook that blocks holds the worker: the other nodes' dt grows. Update at intervals with period, and give a node whose hooks must block (on a device, a socket, a lock) dedicated_thread=True. The host waits with run.timer.sleep, which follows the time scale and the pauses of the run; time.sleep follows neither
  • A node runs once. Running a node or network that has run raises RuntimeError; build new instances to run again. After the run, the attributes stay readable
  • Do not read a node's attributes from the host while it runs. It races with the node's updates. Read the ports with run.read, or take run.state_dict()
  • Send nothing that depends on the state in on_start. A restore loads the state after on_start
  • Do not change the state in on_stop. The state taken after a normal end is the state the nodes left after on_stop. Release resources such as I/O there
  • Register the values that change while running. Tensors and modules are collected by themselves; plain values (a counter, the time last seen) and containers of tensors (a list as a replay buffer) need register_state, or a restore starts them again
  • Keep the graph inside one update. Hooks record gradients as plain PyTorch does. Update the parameters inside torch.no_grad(), and detach a value computed from the parameters before you carry it to the next update in an attribute, or the graph keeps growing
  • After an exception, the time stands still. The run's time stops when the run ends, so self.timer does not move in on_exception and on_stop: measure real time there (to slow a robot down over a second, say)
  • Only the host moves the time, and only through ports does a node talk. In a hook, Timer.sleep, pause, resume, set_time_scale, VirtualTimer.advance and the methods of Run raise RuntimeError: a node that moved the time would change the dt of every other node of the run. backward() cannot reach another node, since a sent value is a detached copy

docs.text: Working programs that show how to use Mujou, in examples/ of the repository. The pages of this site include them as they are, so the code shown is the code you can run. They are guides, not tests: the test suite does not run them.

docs.title: What each program shows
docs.text:
• quickstart.py: a two-node network, run with with mujou.run(...). The host writes an input with write, and waits with wait_for until the expected output arrives
  • branching.py: a Port that only sends, connected to two branches that a MultiPort merges; and a MultiPort that sends a different value to each peer with send_to, on the channels connect returned
  • leaky.py: the leaky integrator, a node defined in continuous time and advanced by the exact solution, so that it is stable for any dt. Run, it steps the input of two in a row and compares them with the exact solution at the time each output was sent
  • test_leaky.py: tests of the node of leaky.py with mujou.testing, on a virtual timer with manual steps: against the exact solution, bit for bit against the discrete algorithm, and a resumed run against one that did not stop. Run them with uv run pytest examples/test_leaky.py
  • online_learning.py: a teacher sends batches from y = a x + b with the a the host writes and changes; a learner learns from each new batch with plain PyTorch autograd, for the time since the last one, and the host follows its loss as it falls, jumps and falls again
  • feedback_alignment.py: two nodes learn a two-layer network by feedback alignment: two-way ports, a target relayed with the activity, a learning step once per sample with pc.LearnClock
  • pc_regression.py: pc.Chain and pc.show learn a regression from a stream of batches, measured before each batch is learned from
  • mnist/: a 784-256-256-10 network learns MNIST as a pc.Chain, and the same network learns by BP from the same initial weights on the same batches. main.py is the entry point, data.py loads the data, metrics.py measures, bp.py trains the BP baseline and watch.py counts the dt of the nodes (--watch)
  • save_and_restore.py: takes the state with run.state_dict(), saves it with torch.save, and resumes it in a new instance with mujou.run(..., state=...), on a timer of the resumed run's own
  • group.py: Group(enc=..., dec=...), and the paths of the nodes ("enc.scale")
  • subscribe.py: run.subscribe yields the latest output, then each newer one, and stops with break
  • timers.py: Timestamp, a Timer of a run's own at a time scale, the scale of the global timer, and pausing the global timer to take the states of two runs at one time; a run resumed from one goes on on a timer of its own
  • errors.py: the NetworkError the host receives and its __cause__, the order on_exception → on_stop, and mujou.run raising for an exception in on_start

docs.title: How to run them
docs.text:
Run them from the root of the repository, in an environment built from source (see Installation).

uv run python examples/quickstart.py
uv run python examples/mnist/main.py

None of the programs uses a GPU. Each finishes within 15 seconds, except mnist/: it downloads MNIST (about 11 MB) on its first run, and its defaults (3 epochs) take about 2 minutes.

docs.title: 📦 Installation
docs.text:
Not on PyPI yet

Mujou is not on PyPI yet. For now, build it from source.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Details Python 3.14 or later. The free-threaded build 3.14t is recommended. The regular 3.14 build with the GIL also works PyTorch Installed automatically as a dependency of Mujou Rust 1.85 or later, installed with rustup. Needed only to build from source uv uv. Needed only to build from source

The free-threaded build is recommended because the nodes run on several worker threads at once. With the GIL, nodes written in Python compete for the GIL and rarely run in parallel.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Geson-anko/mujou.git
cd mujou
uv sync

uv sync sets up the free-threaded Python 3.14t, creates .venv/, installs the dependencies (with what the example programs need, such as numpy), and builds the core, which is written in Rust. For the regular build with the GIL, run uv sync --python 3.14 instead.

uv sync installs PyTorch from PyPI, like the other dependencies. To use another build, such as a CPU-only one or another CUDA version, follow the PyTorch installation guide.

After the release on PyPI

These commands will work once Mujou is on PyPI: uv add mujou in a uv project, or pip install mujou in a virtual environment with Python 3.14 or later.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
uv run python -c "import mujou; print(mujou.__version__)"  # prints a version such as 0.0.1
uv run python examples/quickstart.py  # prints a line such as: y = tensor([3., 5., 7.]) at t = 0.017 s

The first page of the tutorial explains the second program and its output.

docs.title: mujou.Network
docs.text:
Bases: Component

A composite of nodes and other networks, declared as attributes.

Assign nodes and networks as attributes and connect their ports with Port.connect. The children of a network are the nodes and networks among its attributes, in the order of assignment: mujou.run reads them when it starts, as nn.Module finds its submodules, so nodes in a list, a tuple or a dict are not children (the run raises TypeError for them). A port assigned to a network is only a reference to it: expose the ports the host uses that way (by convention prev and next, e.g. self.prev = self.l1.prev). A network is only the structure of a run: its nodes still run independently and asynchronously.

mujou.run(net) runs the network; the Run it returns is how the host talks to the running nodes. A node of the network is at the path of its attributes from the root ("body.l1"), which names it in the state tree and in errors.

Example::

class Stack(Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.l1 = Hidden(784, 256)
        self.l2 = Hidden(256, 256)
        self.l1.next.connect(self.l2.prev)
        self.prev = self.l1.prev  # expose the previous side
        self.next = self.l2.next  # expose the next side


class Classifier(Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.body = Stack()
        self.head = Head()  # a node with prev, next and teacher ports
        self.body.next.connect(self.head.prev)  # l2.next <-> head.prev
        self.prev = self.body.prev  # the input
        self.teacher = self.head.teacher  # the target, a port of head


net = Classifier()
with mujou.run(net, inputs={net.prev: x0, net.teacher: y0}) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x, net.teacher: y})  # switch together
    run.timer.sleep(0.1)  # present the input for 0.1 s of the run's time
    prediction = run.read(net.head.next)
    state = run.state_dict()

docs.title: mujou.Group
docs.text:
Group(**children: Node | Network)

Bases: Network

A network of the given nodes and networks side by side, each at its keyword, unconnected unless they were connected before.

The node l1 of Group(enc=a) is at "enc.l1".

Example::

enc, dec = Encoder(), Decoder()
enc.next.connect(dec.prev)
with mujou.run(Group(enc=enc, dec=dec)) as run:
    state = run.state_dict()  # nodes "enc.l1", ..., "dec.l1", ...

docs.title: mujou.Node
docs.text:
Node(
    *,
    period: float = 0.01,
    seed: int | None = None,
    device: device | str = "cpu",
    dedicated_thread: bool = False,
)

Bases: Component

A unit of asynchronous computation: the leaf of a network.

Call super().__init__(...) first in __init__ (mujou.run raises TypeError for a node that did not), then declare the node's ports and state as attributes of the instance. A run reads the attributes when it starts. A node must not hold other nodes or networks as attributes, nor ports in a list, a tuple or a dict (the run raises TypeError); put nodes side by side in a Network instead.

Override the lifecycle hooks below; each does nothing by default. As in any subclass, call the same hook of super() first in each override. The framework calls the hooks on the thread that runs the node (see "Threads" below), in this order:

  • on_start(): once, when the run starts (also when it is restored). Open the node's I/O here. A node with dedicated_thread=True gets it on its own thread, so it can also make its per-thread settings here. Do not send anything that depends on the state here: a restore loads the state after it.
  • load_state_dict(state): only when the run was restored, after on_start and before the first on_update.
  • on_update(dt): repeatedly, once every period on average (see below). dt is the time in seconds on the run's timer since the node's last update. Read the ports with recv, update in proportion to dt, and write the ports with send. It never waits for other nodes.
  • on_pause(): when the node has stopped for the run to take its state (Run.state_dict). on_resume(): when that pause ends, before the next on_update. A pause of the timer (Timer.pause) calls neither: the node only sees no time pass.
  • on_exception(): once on every node, when a hook of any node has raised, before on_stop.
  • on_stop(): once, when the run stops, also after an exception. It must not change what state_dict returns: the state taken after a normal end is the state at the stop.

state_dict() is called when the run's state is taken, while the node is paused (or, after a normal end, on the host's thread that called Run.state_dict). Its ports refuse to receive or send there, so that taking the state is not seen by the other nodes. The framework copies what it returns before the node resumes.

The state of a node is, as for an nn.Module, every attribute that holds a torch.Tensor (nn.Parameter included) or an object with state_dict and load_state_dict (an nn.Module, a pc.LearnClock; not a class), every attribute registered with register_state, and the state of generator. What an attribute holds when the state is taken or loaded decides. The settings that __init__ computes from its arguments (a time constant, say) are no state: a node restored with other arguments keeps its own. Register the plain values that change while the node runs (a counter, the time last seen), and the containers of tensors (a list as a replay buffer, a dict of tensors): a list or a dict is no state by itself, even of tensors. Make the state in __init__ and update it in place: load_state_dict copies into the tensors that the node holds. To choose the state yourself, override both state_dict and load_state_dict: extend what super().state_dict() returns, and pass super().load_state_dict the state without the keys you added.

If any hook raises, the whole run stops. A hook must not call mujou.run or the methods of any Run (write, read, state_dict, ...): they raise RuntimeError there, because a node talks only through its own ports.

Threads: by default the node runs on the workers, a pool of threads that the run shares among its nodes (mujou.run(..., workers=...)). Each hook may then run on a different thread from the previous one, but the hooks of a node never run at the same time, and each sees what the previous one wrote. Whether the next hook sees what a hook set per thread (threading.local, threading.current_thread(), settings of torch such as torch.set_grad_enabled or torch.autocast) depends on the schedule, and the next node on the same worker may see it too: set such settings back before the hook returns (inside a with, say). contextvars do persist: each node runs its hooks in a contextvars.Context of its own, which starts empty (it does not inherit the host's). A hook that blocks (time.sleep, waiting for I/O or a lock) holds its worker meanwhile, and the other nodes' dt grows; give such a node dedicated_thread=True, so that it runs on a thread of its own, with every hook on that thread.

The framework leaves gradient recording as it is, on by default as in plain PyTorch: a hook may call backward directly, and computes without a graph inside with torch.no_grad():. No graph crosses nodes: a port sends a detached copy. Before each hook, when device is CUDA, the framework makes the device and a stream of the node's own current: the only per-thread settings it makes, and around state_dict (which may run on the host's thread) it sets the thread's own back. On CUDA it also waits for the work queued on that stream after on_update (holding its worker meanwhile), after load_state_dict and around state_dict. It does this around the hooks, so overriding one never skips it.

The node updates once every period (0.01 s by default) of the run's timer on average: the time an update takes counts toward the period, and a node that falls a whole period behind does not update several times in a row to catch up. A pause does not count. dt is still the time that actually passed since the last update, longer than period when the node is late, so keep updating in proportion to it and stay stable for the longest dt it can get. A manual run (ManualRun.step) ignores the period.

period=0.0 updates as soon as any time has passed since the last update. Set it only when the node must: such a node keeps a CPU core busy, and takes time from the other nodes, whose dt it makes irregular. period=math.inf never updates by itself: only ManualRun.step updates such a node.

Example::

class Hidden(Node):
    def __init__(self, n_in: int, n_out: int) -> None:
        super().__init__(seed=0)
        x, h = TensorSpec((32, n_in)), TensorSpec((32, n_out))
        # Send W^T eps back and receive x from the previous side (one peer).
        self.prev = Port(send=x, recv=x)
        # Send h forward and receive W^T eps from each next peer (many).
        self.next = MultiPort(send=h, recv=h)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # torch.Tensor
        feedback = self.next.recv()  # dict[Channel, torch.Tensor]
        ...
        self.next.send(h)
        self.prev.send(wt_eps)


l1, l2 = Hidden(784, 256), Hidden(256, 256)
l1.next.connect(l2.prev)
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION period

The time between two updates on average, in seconds of the run's timer. 0.0 updates as soon as any time has passed.

TYPE: float DEFAULT: 0.01

seed

The seed of generator. None seeds it nondeterministically.

TYPE: int | None DEFAULT: None

device

Where the node computes: the CPU or a CUDA device (no other device type is supported). Received messages arrive on it. "cuda" without an index is fixed to the host's current CUDA device.

TYPE: device | str DEFAULT: 'cpu'

dedicated_thread

Run the node on a thread of its own instead of the run's workers: for a node whose hooks block, or that relies on per-thread state set once (in on_start).

TYPE: bool DEFAULT: False

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

device is neither the CPU nor a CUDA device, or is CUDA while CUDA is not available, or period is negative or NaN.

docs.text:
device: device

The device the node computes on and receives messages on.

Allocate with it (torch.zeros(..., device=self.device)): the current device in the hooks is this one, but an explicit device states the intent.

docs.title: dedicated_thread property
docs.text:
dedicated_thread: bool

Whether the node runs on a thread of its own instead of the run's workers.

docs.title: generator property
docs.text:
generator: Generator

The node's own random generator on device, seeded with seed.

seed sets nothing else: use this generator instead of the global one, which all nodes share (do not call torch.manual_seed in a node), also to initialize modules (nn.init.normal_(w, generator=self.generator)). super().__init__ creates it, so it can be used in __init__ already, and the hooks go on with the same sequence. Its state is part of the node's state, so a restored node goes on with the same sequence too.

docs.title: timer property
docs.text:
timer: ReadOnlyTimer

The reading side of the timer of the run whose hook runs, which measures the dt of its nodes.

Read the time with self.timer.now() in the hooks (state_dict included). The timer is the one given to mujou.run(..., timer=...), the global timer by default, or, for a run restored from a state, a new timer that started at the time of the state (Run.timer). A ReadOnlyTimer only reads: a node does not change the time of its run (Timer.sleep, set_time_scale and VirtualTimer.advance raise RuntimeError in a hook). It stops at the time the run ends, so the hooks that run after the end (on_exception, on_stop) see the time stand still; measure real time there instead. The host reads Run.timer.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

This is not read in a hook of this node while it runs (but in __init__, by the host, or by another node).

docs.title: register_state
docs.text:
register_state(name: str) -> None

Add the attribute name to the state, whatever value it holds.

Use it for the plain values that change while the node runs (a counter, the time last seen) and for the containers of tensors (a list as a replay buffer), which are not state by themselves. The attribute is state while it is assigned, whatever it holds. The default state_dict returns the value as it is, and the default load_state_dict assigns a deep copy of the saved value (or copies into a tensor, or loads into an object with load_state_dict, that the attribute holds then).

Register in __init__: a restore loads into new instances, which must have the same state.

The state is data: when the run takes it, it detaches every tensor of what state_dict returns (in its dicts, lists and tuples) and copies the result, so no graph goes with it.

torch.load(..., weights_only=True) reads only basic types (int, float, bool, str, None, and lists, tuples and dicts of them and of tensors): keep the registered values to those if the state is saved with torch.save.

RAISES DESCRIPTION AttributeError

The node has no attribute name (not assigned yet, misspelled, or a property); assign it first.

docs.title: on_start
docs.text:
on_start() -> None

Called once when the run starts (also when it is restored), before any other hook. Do not send anything that depends on the state here: a restore loads it later.

docs.title: on_update
docs.text:
on_update(dt: float) -> None

Called repeatedly with dt, the seconds on the run's timer since the node's last update (always > 0). Read the ports, update in proportion to dt and send.

docs.title: on_pause
docs.text:
on_pause() -> None

Called when the node has stopped for the run to take its state (Run.state_dict), at the end of its current on_update. A pause of the timer (Timer.pause) does not call it.

docs.title: on_resume
docs.text:
on_resume() -> None

Called when the pause for taking the state ends, before the next on_update.

docs.title: on_exception
docs.text:
on_exception() -> None

Called once on every node when a hook of any node has raised, before on_stop. What it raises is logged and ignored.

docs.title: on_stop
docs.text:
on_stop() -> None

Called once when the run stops, also after an exception. It must not change what state_dict returns. What it raises is logged and ignored.

docs.title: state_dict
docs.text:
state_dict() -> dict[str, Any]

Return the node's state: "generator", the state of generator, then each attribute of the state in the order of assignment, under its name: a tensor detach-ed, the state_dict() of an object that has one, or a registered value as it is.

The tensors share memory with the attributes (the framework copies the tree). requires_grad and .grad are not part of the state, as in nn.Module.state_dict.

docs.title: load_state_dict
docs.text:
load_state_dict(state: Mapping[str, Any]) -> None

Restore state, as the default state_dict returned it, into the attributes of the state, without recording gradients: copy_ into each tensor, load_state_dict into each object that has one, and assign a copy.deepcopy of the saved value to any other registered attribute, with the tensors in it (in its dicts, lists and tuples) moved to device.

The objects stay the same, so references taken in __init__ or on_start see the restored values, and a tensor that records gradients stays a leaf that does. copy_ casts the dtype and moves the device. The state of generator is set as it is saved, and a generator keeps its state in a format of its device's type: the state must come from a node on the same type of device (the CPU or CUDA).

An override that keeps a tensor of state as it is shares its memory with the tree given to mujou.run(..., state=...): copy it instead.

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

The keys of state are not those of this node's state, or a tensor's shape differs.

docs.title: mujou.Port
docs.text:
Port(
    *,
    send: MessageSpec[S] | None = None,
    recv: MessageSpec[R] | None = None,
    initial: S | None = None,
)

Bases: _Port[S, R]

A connection point that sends messages of type S and receives at most one peer's messages of type R.

Declare ports as attributes of a node in __init__. send is the spec of what the port sends and recv the spec of what it receives; omit one for a one-way port (its message type is then Never). recv() returns one message, so a port that receives takes one peer; a port that only sends takes any number, and send reaches them all. To receive from several peers of one kind, use a MultiPort; for inputs of different roles, use one port each.

Two ports connect when the send of each equals the recv of the other. A port may stay unconnected: the host then writes what it receives (Run.write).

initial is what the port has sent before its first send: what its peers receive and the host reads until then. A run copies it when it starts. Without it, that is the zeros() of send. A restored run takes the values from the state instead.

A run names the port in its errors by the path of its node and its attribute ("body.l1.next"; "Shift.next" for a port of the node run as the root).

Example::

class Sensor(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.next = Port(send=TensorSpec((3,)), initial=torch.ones(3))


class Monitor(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = Port(recv=TensorSpec((3,)))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()  # torch.Tensor; ones until the sensor sends


sensor, monitor = Sensor(), Monitor()
sensor.next.connect(monitor.prev)

The spec of the messages this port sends, or None.

docs.title: recv_spec property
docs.text:
recv_spec: MessageSpec[R] | None

The spec of the messages this port receives, or None.

docs.title: initial property
docs.text:
initial: S | None

What the port has sent before its first send, or None for the zeros() of its send spec.

The channels of this port, in the order they were connected.

docs.title: connect
docs.text:
connect(other: Port[R, S] | MultiPort[R, S]) -> Channel

Connect this port to other and return the channel between them.

The channel is registered at both ports, so each sends to and receives from the other. Connecting the same two ports again, in either order, returns the same channel. A port may connect to itself.

RAISES DESCRIPTION TypeError

The specs are not mutually reversed: self.send_spec != other.recv_spec or self.recv_spec != other.send_spec.

ValueError

A Port that receives would get a second peer (use a MultiPort to receive from several).

docs.title: send
docs.text:
send(msg: S) -> None

Send msg to every peer and to what the host reads (Run.read).

msg must match the send spec exactly; dtypes are never converted. The values are detached and copied, so changing msg afterwards changes nothing that was sent. A CUDA tensor is copied to the host on the node's stream. It never waits for the peers to read.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

The caller is not a hook of the node that owns the port, while it runs (or is its state_dict).

TypeError

A value is not a torch.Tensor, or a DictSpec message is not a dict with the spec's keys.

ValueError

A shape or a dtype differs from the spec.

BufferError

A tensor is not dense (torch.strided).

docs.title: recv
docs.text:
recv() -> R

Return the latest message received, without waiting for a new one.

The message comes from the peer's send; an unconnected port reads what the host writes with Run.write instead. Until that writer first writes, it is the initial value: the peer port's initial, or else the recv spec's zeros(). For a port the host writes, it is the value in inputs of mujou.run, or else the zeros(). A restored run takes it from state. recv_with_time tells whether the writer has written yet.

Every call copies into new tensors on the owning node's device, without gradients, so changing them in place changes nothing else.

RAISES DESCRIPTION RuntimeError

The caller is not a hook of the node that owns the port, while it runs (or is its state_dict).

docs.title: recv_with_time
docs.text:
recv_with_time() -> tuple[R, _native.Timestamp | None]

Like recv, but return (message, time).

time is the Timestamp on the run's timer at which the writer wrote the message, or None while the writer has not written yet (the message is then the initial value). The writer is the peer (its send or send_to), or the host for an unconnected port (inputs of mujou.run or Run.write). A restored run keeps the times of the state, None included. Raises as recv does.

docs.title: mujou.MultiPort
docs.text:
MultiPort(
    *,
    send: MessageSpec[S] | None = None,
    recv: MessageSpec[R] | None = None,
    initial: S | None = None,
)

Bases: _Port[S, R]

A connection point that sends messages of type S and receives messages of type R from any number of peers of one kind.

It is declared and connected as a Port is, but recv() returns {channel: message}, one entry per peer in connection order, and send_to sends to one peer. Use it to merge or to branch peers that play the same role; for inputs of different roles (a prediction and an error, say), use one Port each. The host does not write to a MultiPort.

Example::

class Sum(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = MultiPort(recv=TensorSpec((3,)))
        self.next = Port(send=TensorSpec((3,)))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(sum(self.prev.recv().values(), torch.zeros(3)))

Channel(a: AnyPort, b: AnyPort)

One connection between two ports, which connect makes.

A channel is the handle of a peer: a MultiPort's recv is keyed by channel, and send_to takes one. A channel made otherwise connects nothing.

Example::

ch = a.next.connect(b.prev)
ch.other(a.next) is b.prev  # True

docs.title: mujou.TensorSpec
docs.text:
TensorSpec(shape: Sequence[int], dtype: dtype = torch.float32)

Bases: MessageSpec[Tensor]

The shape and the dtype of a message that is one torch.Tensor.

Every dimension is at least 1, and () is a scalar. A batch dimension is just a part of the shape.

Two specs are equal when their shapes and dtypes are equal. A message whose shape or dtype differs from the spec is an error; dtypes are never converted. A spec has no device: a message of the spec may be on any device.

zeros, rand and empty make a tensor of the spec, on the CPU unless device says otherwise. For any other initial value, fill one of them in place (spec.empty().fill_(0.5)).

Example::

spec = TensorSpec((32, 256))  # float32
spec = TensorSpec((32, 256), torch.bfloat16)
x0 = spec.zeros()
noise = TensorSpec((4,)).rand(generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
ones = spec.empty(device="cuda").fill_(1.0)
RAISES DESCRIPTION TypeError

dtype is not in dtypes.

docs.text:
DictSpec(typed_dict: type[TD], /, **specs: TensorSpec)

Bases: MessageSpec[TD]

The spec of a message that is a TypedDict of torch.Tensor values.

Give the TypedDict class and one TensorSpec per key. Every key of the TypedDict is required and annotated as torch.Tensor (no nesting), and the keyword arguments name exactly its keys. The keys keep the order in which the TypedDict defines them.

Two specs are equal when they use the same TypedDict class and equal TensorSpec for every key.

Example::

class Feedback(TypedDict):
    error: torch.Tensor
    target: torch.Tensor


spec = DictSpec(
    Feedback, error=TensorSpec((32, 256)), target=TensorSpec((32, 10))
)
msg: Feedback = spec.zeros()
RAISES DESCRIPTION TypeError

The keyword arguments miss a key of the TypedDict or name a key it does not have.

docs.title: mujou.pc
docs.text:
PC-ALM (augmented Lagrangian predictive coding) as nodes of mujou.

Each node holds a part of the model and learns from its neighbors' messages only: Input takes the samples the host writes, each Layer wraps a module as one constraint h = f(h_in), and Output holds the last module and the loss. Inside a node, the module is differentiated by autograd; between nodes, activities (Activity) flow to the next node and gradients of the energy to the previous one. The target of each sample travels with its input in the Activity, so the output node pairs every prediction with its own target. Chain connects the nodes for a sequence of modules, and show shows it a sample. Each node gives the spec of what it sends as act_spec, which the next node takes, to build other shapes by hand. MSELoss and CrossEntropyLoss give the loss of each sample. LearnClock and functional hold the parts the nodes are made of, for writing nodes of your own.

The samples are independent and the shapes start with the batch, batch: () (the default) for one sample at a time, B for B samples, or a shape of several dimensions.

Import it as a submodule::

import mujou.pc as pc

B = 64
net = pc.Chain(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU()),
    nn.Linear(256, 10),
    x=TensorSpec((B, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((B,), torch.int64),
    batch=B,
    loss=pc.CrossEntropyLoss(B),
    tau=pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=8e-3, theta=1.28),
    learn_interval=0.15,
)

docs.title: Size
docs.text: Size = int | tuple[int, ...]

docs.title: Chain
docs.text:
Chain(
    *modules: Module,
    x: TensorSpec,
    y: TensorSpec,
    loss: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor],
    tau: TimeConstants,
    learn_interval: float | None,
    batch: Size = (),
    max_dt: float | None = None,
    device: device | str = "cpu",
)

Bases: Network

Input -> Layer -> ... -> Output: a network that learns modules in sequence by PC-ALM, as nn.Sequential(*modules) would compute them.

modules[:-1] each become a Layer and modules[-1] the Output, after an Input of the samples x and targets y. Each node takes the act_spec of the one before and the nodes are connected in order. The children are input, layer0, ..., output (modules[i] is in layer{i}, also layers[i]), which are also their paths in Run.state_dict(). Every node runs with the period tau.period (tau.h / 4); for other periods, build the nodes one by one (show shows them samples too).

The host writes a Sample to prev and reads a Prediction from next, or does both with show.

Example::

B = 64
net = pc.Chain(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU()),
    nn.Linear(256, 10),
    x=TensorSpec((B, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((B,), torch.int64),
    batch=B,
    loss=pc.CrossEntropyLoss(B),
    tau=pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=8e-3, theta=1.28),
    learn_interval=0.15,
)
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    prediction = pc.show(run, net, sample, seconds=0.2)
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION modules

The functions of the nodes, in order, on device.

TYPE: Module DEFAULT: ()

x

The spec of the inputs, (*batch, *in).

TYPE: TensorSpec

y

The spec of the targets, (*batch, *target).

TYPE: TensorSpec

loss

The loss of each sample, as in Output.

TYPE: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor]

tau

The time constants of every node.

TYPE: TimeConstants

learn_interval

As in Layer. Longer than the round trip of the credit, 2 * len(modules) * tau.period, is recommended.

TYPE: float | None

batch

The batch, as in Input: () for one sample, B for B samples.

TYPE: Size DEFAULT: ()

max_dt

As in Layer.

TYPE: float | None DEFAULT: None

device

Where the nodes compute.

TYPE: device | str DEFAULT: 'cpu'

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

As Input, Layer and Output raise.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
Input(
    *,
    x: TensorSpec,
    y: TensorSpec,
    period: float,
    batch: Size = (),
    device: device | str = "cpu",
)

Bases: Node

A node that takes the samples the host writes and sends them on as the Activity of the next node, with their targets.

The host writes a Sample (x, y and mask) to prev with Run.write. In each on_update the node sends from next an Activity whose h is x, with y, mask and the time (ns) at which the host wrote them: the nodes on the path pass them on with the activity computed from x, so that the output node pairs each prediction with its own target. A new time tells them the input changed. jumps counts the writes the node has seen, so that the next node moves its h with a new x even when it was written at the same time as the zeros before it (time 0). x is clamped: what the next node sends back on next is not read.

Before the host first writes, the node sends zeros with mask False, jumps 0 and time 0. The state holds "jumps" and the time (ns) of the last write seen ("seen_write", None before any). act_spec is the spec of what the node sends, for the next node.

Example::

B = 64
inp = pc.Input(
    x=TensorSpec((B, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((B,), torch.int64),
    period=1e-3,
    batch=B,
)
...
mask = torch.ones(B, dtype=torch.bool)
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({inp.prev: {"x": x, "y": y, "mask": mask}})
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION x

The spec of the inputs x, (*batch, *in).

TYPE: TensorSpec

y

The spec of the targets y, (*batch, *target).

TYPE: TensorSpec

period

The period of the node in seconds, usually that of the next node.

TYPE: float

batch

The batch that x and y start with, as in activity_spec: () for one sample, B for B samples.

TYPE: Size DEFAULT: ()

device

Where the node computes.

TYPE: device | str DEFAULT: 'cpu'

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

x or y does not start with batch.

docs.title: Layer
docs.text:
Layer(
    module: Module,
    *,
    act_spec: DictSpec[Activity],
    tau: TimeConstants,
    learn_interval: float | None,
    period: float | None = None,
    max_dt: float | None = None,
    device: device | str = "cpu",
)

Bases: Node

A node that wraps module as one constraint h = f(h_in; theta) of PC-ALM.

It predicts mu = module(h_in) from the activity h_in of the previous node, and holds its own activity h, which it sends to the next nodes, and the dual lam of the constraint. With \(r = h - \mu\), \(\delta = r + \lambda\) and the sum \(g\) of what the next nodes send back:

\[ \tau_h \dot h = -(r + \lambda + g),\qquad \tau_\lambda \dot\lambda = r,\qquad \tau_\theta \dot\theta = -g_\theta / B, \]

where \(B\) is the number of samples in the batch (1 without one), \(g_\theta = -J_\theta^\top \delta\) and the node sends \(g_{\mathrm{in}} = -J_h^\top \delta\) to the previous node (both from one vector-Jacobian product of module, functional.vjp). At a fixed point, \(r = 0\) (h is the forward pass) and lam is the credit \(-\partial\ell/\partial h\) of backpropagation. Inside the node, module is differentiated by autograd; between nodes, only these messages flow.

h follows the gradient flow above, with the mu of the moment: when the nodes below relax, h_in and mu move continuously and h only relaxes towards them. Where mu jumps, h moves with it once, so that the deviation r = h - mu and lam are kept, and only they are:

  • With a new sample (the time of the activity changed), or when the h_in it reads jumped (its jumps changed), the node moves h <- mu + (h - mu_last) with the mu_last of its previous update. Without a target, h is thus the forward pass.
  • When it updates theta, it computes once more, without gradients, mu' = f(h_in; theta_new) at the same h_in, and moves h <- h + (mu' - mu) at the start of its next update, with mu_last <- mu'. Only the jump that theta makes moves h, not the drift of h_in. The move waits one update so that the next nodes, which may read h before they learn, see it as a jump (it is sent with new jumps) rather than learn from it.

The node advances its jumps once in an update that moves h with a new sample or a jump of h_in, or by a jump of theta while learn_interval is set; the next node then moves with it in turn, so a jump runs up the path with r unchanged at every node, whenever each node learns. With learn_interval=None, theta moves by dt in every update, continuously: the node moves its own h but does not advance its jumps, as moving every node above in every update would hold r rather than h as the state, which diverges in deep chains.

Each on_update(dt):

  1. reads the activity and ticks its clock, which caps dt at max_dt;
  2. moves h by the jump of theta of the previous update, if any;
  3. computes mu, g_in and, when it learns, g_theta with the delta before this update, zero for the samples whose mask is False, and sends g_in;
  4. with a new input or new jumps of h_in, moves h with mu; then moves h and then lam by dt with the g the next nodes sent (functional.relax_);
  5. sends h with its jumps, and the y, mask and time that came with h_in;
  6. when it learns, moves theta by the time since its last update (functional.learn_) and computes the jump of mu it made.

Its clock (a LearnClock) tells when it learns: in its first update once learn_interval seconds have passed since the host wrote the input (its time, on the run's time), and then every learn_interval seconds while the input stays, but never in the update that first sees an input (its delta is still that of the input before); with learn_interval=None, in every update; with tau.theta infinite, never (LearnClock.of). The nodes read the one timer of the run, so the nodes on a path learn at about the same time, however deep they are, and each from the relaxed delta of the same input. A learn_interval longer than the round trip of the credit down the path and back (2 * hops * period, with hops the number of connections from the Input to the Output) is recommended: with intervals of a few periods, every node learns, and so advances its jumps, in almost every update, the nodes above move h with every change of mu, and deep chains have been seen to diverge however slowly theta moves. The node does not learn when no sample of the input has a target (every mask is False): that time is dropped from the next update, which would otherwise learn from the delta left over from an earlier input. Nor does it keep the time of an input that changed before the node learned from it. Until the first sample reaches the node, the activity is zeros (mask all False, time 0), so it does not learn then.

dt is capped because the nodes are coupled explicitly: g was made from h as it was when the next node last updated. After a long stall (a loaded machine), the step dt / tau.h of every node grows at once and the coupling makes the network diverge, which no split of the step inside the node prevents. The time beyond max_dt is dropped, from the relaxation and from the weight of the next update of theta alike. The default tau.max_dt, min(tau.h / 2, 3 * tau.lam), keeps the step of h and lam stable in the node itself.

module must treat the samples of the batch independently (no BatchNorm in training mode): the gradient of each sample must be its own. It must also be deterministic and keep no state of its own (no Dropout, no BatchNorm in training mode): an update that learns calls it once more on the same h_in to find the jump of theta, which would otherwise add noise, or update running statistics a second time. Its parameters that require gradients learn; set requires_grad to False to freeze one. It is called once on zeros when the node is made, to find the shape and dtype of h.

The state (Run.state_dict()["nodes"][path]["state"]) holds "generator" (the state of the node's generator), "module" (its state_dict), "h" and "lam" ((*batch, *out)), the prediction of the last update ("mu"), the jump of theta still to add to h ("jump", and "jumped" whether there is one), the jumps it sends and the last ones it read ("jumps", "seen_jumps") and when to learn ("clock", the state of the LearnClock). To watch the node while it runs, read them there: Run.state_dict() pauses the run, whereas reading module, h or lam from the host's thread races with the node's updates in place. act_spec is the spec of what the node sends, for the next node.

Example::

B = 64
tau = pc.TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=8e-3, theta=1.28)
inp = pc.Input(
    x=TensorSpec((B, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((B,), torch.int64),
    period=tau.period,
    batch=B,
)
hidden = pc.Layer(
    nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU()),
    act_spec=inp.act_spec,
    tau=tau,
    learn_interval=24e-3,
)
inp.next.connect(hidden.prev)
hidden.next.connect(out.prev)  # out: a pc.Output, or another pc.Layer

The function f, (*batch, *in) -> (*batch, *out), on device.

tau

TYPE: TimeConstants

learn_interval

The time in seconds from the write of an input to the update of theta, and between the updates while the input stays; longer than 2 * hops * period is recommended. None updates in every on_update, for a stream whose input changes at every frame (good values for it have not been measured yet); math.inf never updates.

TYPE: float | None

The period of the node in seconds; None is tau.period (tau.h / 4). It must not be longer than max_dt.

max_dt

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Output(
    module: Module,
    *,
    act_spec: DictSpec[Activity],
    loss: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor],
    tau: TimeConstants,
    learn_interval: float | None,
    period: float | None = None,
    max_dt: float | None = None,
    device: device | str = "cpu",
)

Bases: Node

A node that predicts y_hat = module(h_in) and whose energy is the loss of the samples that have a target.

It pairs h_in with the target y and mask of the same Activity, so the prediction always meets the target of the very input it was computed from, however fast the host writes. With

\[ \ell = \sum_b \mathrm{mask}_b\, \ell_b(\hat y_b, y_b),\qquad \tau_\theta \dot\theta = -\frac{1}{B}\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\theta}, \]

where \(B\) is the number of samples in the batch (1 without one), it sends \(g_{\mathrm{in}} = \partial\ell/\partial h_{\mathrm{in}}\) to the previous node (functional.loss_vjp): zero for a sample without a target while its y_hat is finite. Each on_update(dt) caps dt at max_dt as Layer does, reads the Activity, sends g_in, sends a Prediction (y_hat with the y, mask and time it was paired with) for the host to read, and updates theta when it learns. It does not read the jumps: a jump of h_in needs no move here, as the node holds no activity of its own.

It learns as Layer does, by its clock: once learn_interval seconds have passed since the host wrote the input, but not in the update that first sees it, or in every update with None. When no sample has a target, it does not learn and drops the time since the last update; so too before the first sample arrives, while the activity is zeros (mask all False), and when the input changes before it has learned from it. B is the number of samples in the batch, not the number of samples with a target: a sample without one adds zero.

loss returns the loss of each sample, of the shape of the batch (that of mask), such as MSELoss(batch) or CrossEntropyLoss(batch), and the node sums them. A loss that averages over the batch (such as nn.MSELoss()) would scale the gradient that flows back by 1 / B, so the node refuses it when it is made: it calls module and loss once on zeros then (functional.loss_vjp), which also finds the shape of y_hat. module must treat the samples independently, as in Layer.

The state holds "generator", "module" and when to learn ("clock"). Read it with Run.state_dict(), as for Layer.

Example::

out = pc.Output(
    nn.Linear(256, 10),
    act_spec=hidden.act_spec,  # hidden: a pc.Layer
    loss=pc.CrossEntropyLoss(B),
    tau=tau,
    learn_interval=24e-3,
)
hidden.next.connect(out.prev)
# The host: prediction = run.read(out.next); prediction["y_hat"], ...

The function f, (*batch, *in) -> (*batch, *out), on device.

The loss of each sample, (y_hat, y) -> batch.

TYPE: Callable[[Tensor, Tensor], Tensor]

The time constants; tau.theta is used, and the defaults of period and max_dt.

TYPE: TimeConstants

learn_interval

As in Layer.

TYPE: float | None

period

The period of the node in seconds; None is tau.period (tau.h / 4). It must not be longer than max_dt.

TYPE: float | None DEFAULT: None

max_dt

As in Layer: the longest dt an update counts, here towards the weight of the update of theta. The default tau.max_dt is that of Layer, so that every node of a chain counts the same time.

TYPE: float | None DEFAULT: None

device

Where the node computes.

TYPE: device | str DEFAULT: 'cpu'

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

LearnClock raises, as in Layer, or loss does not return the shape of the batch for the output of module and the target.

docs.title: TimeConstants dataclass
docs.text:
TimeConstants(*, h: float, lam: float, theta: float)

The time constants of the continuous-time PC-ALM, in seconds.

A node relaxes its activity h, its dual lam and its parameters theta with

\[ \tau_h \dot h = -(r + \lambda + g),\qquad \tau_\lambda \dot\lambda = r,\qquad \tau_\theta \dot\theta = -g_\theta / B \]

(\(r = h - \mu\)), and a step of dt seconds moves them by dt / tau of the right-hand side (the discrete step sizes are eta_h = dt / h, alpha = dt / lam and eta_theta = dt / theta). One update of theta that weighs elapsed seconds is thus one step of SGD on the mean gradient of the batch with the learning rate elapsed / theta.

lam=math.inf makes the dual stay at zero (alpha = 0, plain predictive coding), and theta=math.inf makes the parameters stay where they are (no learning). h must be finite.

The fields are keyword-only: all three are floats, and a swap by position could not be caught by the type checker.

Example::

tau = TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=8e-3, theta=1.28)
pc_only = TimeConstants(h=4e-3, lam=math.inf, theta=1.28)
RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

h is not finite and > 0, or lam or theta is not

0 (NaN is not).

docs.text:
period: float

The default period of a node, h / 4: a step of h of eta_h = 0.25 per update, about that of the official implementation of PC-ALM, and well within the measured stable range eta_h <= 0.5 (specs/pc.md).

docs.title: max_dt property
docs.text:
max_dt: float

The default longest dt an update counts, min(h / 2, 3 * lam): the explicit Euler step of h then lam is stable for dt / h <= 1/2 and dt / lam <= 3 (specs/pc.md, "dt の打ち切り"). Every node of a chain caps at the same time, so that they weigh their updates of theta alike.

docs.title: LearnClock
docs.text:
LearnClock(*, period: float, learn_interval: float | None, max_dt: float)

Decides, update by update, when a node updates its parameters, from the time the host wrote the node's input.

The node calls tick(dt, time_ns, now_ns) once in each update, with the dt of the update, the time (ns) the input it received was written at, and the time now (ns) on the run's timer. The clock learns in the first update at or after time_ns + k * learn_interval (k = 1, 2, ...), but never in the update that first sees an input: its gradient is still that of the input before. The nodes on a path read the one timer of the run, so they learn at about the same time, however deep they are. With learn_interval=None, it learns in every update, a new input or not; with math.inf, never.

A Tick with learn counts as learned: the next interval starts there, whether the node updates its parameters or skips them for want of a target. elapsed sums the capped dt since then; an input that changes before the clock learned from it drops that sum, as an input without a target does, or inputs that change faster than learn_interval would pile the time up into one large update. dt is capped at max_dt, and the time beyond it is dropped from elapsed too.

The clock starts as if it had seen no input (no time a host writes at): the first update sees a new input, also one written at time 0.

The state (state_dict()) holds the time of the input seen last ("seen_ns", None before any), the time from which the next update learns ("learn_at_ns"), "elapsed", and whether the clock has learned since the input changed ("learned_input"). An attribute of a node that holds a LearnClock is in the node's state by itself.

It is not tied to PC-ALM: any node that learns from inputs the host writes can use it. LearnClock.of makes the clock of a node of PC-ALM from its time constants.

Example::

self.clock = pc.LearnClock(period=self.period, learn_interval=24e-3,
                           max_dt=2e-3)
# In on_update(dt):
tick = self.clock.tick(dt, int(activity["time"]), self.timer.now().ns)
# ... move by tick.dt; if tick.learn, learn weighted by tick.elapsed.
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION period

The period of the node, in seconds.

TYPE: float

learn_interval

The time in seconds from the write of an input to the first update of the parameters, and between the updates while the input stays. None learns in every update, math.inf never.

TYPE: float | None

max_dt

The longest dt an update counts, in seconds.

TYPE: float

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

learn_interval is neither None nor > 0, max_dt is not > 0, or period is longer than max_dt.

docs.title: discrete property
docs.text:
discrete: bool

Whether the clock learns at intervals (learn_interval is not None), so that each update of the parameters is a jump rather than a step of a continuous flow.

Bases: TypedDict

The activity a node sends to the next nodes, with the target of each of its samples.

The shapes start with the batch, batch: () for one sample, (B,) for B samples, or more dimensions (see activity_spec).

  • h: the activity, (*batch, *out).
  • jumps: () int64, the number of times the sender's h has jumped rather than relaxed continuously: an Input counts the writes of the host, and a Layer counts its moves with a new sample and with a jump of the h it receives, and the jumps of its own theta when it learns at intervals (learn_interval not None). A change tells the receiver to move its own h with its prediction, so that the jump does not enter its deviation h - mu (Layer).
  • y: the target of each sample, (*batch, *target).
  • mask: batch bool, whether each sample has a target. A sample whose mask is False adds nothing to the loss, whatever its y is.
  • time: () int64, the time in nanoseconds that Run.write returned for the input h was computed from; 0 before the host first writes.

y, mask and time come from the Sample the host wrote, and every node passes them on with the h it computed from it, in the same message: the output node pairs each prediction with its own target, however fast the host writes.

docs.title: show
docs.text:
show(run: Run, chain: _Shown, sample: Sample, *, seconds: float) -> Prediction

Return the prediction chain makes for sample before it learns from it (a prequential prediction), after showing it seconds long.

chain is a Chain, or any network of the nodes of mujou.pc that exposes the prev of its Input and the next of its Output. Writes sample to chain.prev, waits for the first prediction the host reads for that write, and returns it once seconds (of run.timer) have passed since the write, while the nodes learn from the sample (Sample.mask True) or only relax towards it (every mask False, as to evaluate, where a seconds that lets the input reach the output is enough). A node learns from a sample from its second update with it on (learn_interval after the write, when set), and the first prediction of the sample is made of the first activities with it, so the prediction comes before learning unless the host reads it later than that.

Nothing moves the timer of a ManualRun, so there it does not return.

Example::

mask = torch.ones(B, dtype=torch.bool)
p = pc.show(run, net, pc.Sample(x=x, y=y, mask=mask), seconds=0.2)
correct = int((p["y_hat"].argmax(1) == y).sum())
RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

A tensor of sample has another shape or dtype than the spec of chain.prev.

TypeError

sample lacks a key, or has one too many.

RuntimeError

The run shut down normally before the prediction.

NetworkError

The run stopped because a node raised.

docs.text:
activity_spec(h: TensorSpec, y: TensorSpec, batch: Size = ()) -> DictSpec[Activity]

Return the spec of an Activity whose h is of the spec h, whose targets are of the spec y and whose samples are batch.

batch is the shape that h and y start with, and that of mask: () (the default) for one sample, B or (B,) for B samples, or more dimensions, such as (E, A) for A agents in each of E environments. The samples must be independent of each other (Layer); a dimension that a module mixes, such as the time of a sequence, belongs to h, not to the batch.

Two calls with equal arguments return equal specs. A node of your own that connects to the nodes of mujou.pc declares its ports with it, or with the act_spec of the node before.

Example::

act = pc.activity_spec(TensorSpec((256,)), TensorSpec((), torch.int64))
act = pc.activity_spec(
    TensorSpec((64, 256)), TensorSpec((64,), torch.int64), batch=64
)
RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

h or y does not start with batch.

docs.title: mujou.pc.functional
docs.text:
The stateless computations of PC-ALM that the nodes of mujou.pc are made of, for writing nodes of your own (such as one with several inputs).

A node i predicts mu = f(h_in; theta) from the activity h_in of the previous node, and keeps its activity h and the dual lam of the constraint h = mu. Its energy is E = 0.5 * ||h - mu + lam||^2 (r = h - mu, delta = r + lam).

  • vjp gives the gradients of E with respect to h_in and theta (one vector-Jacobian product inside the node). The node sends the one of h_in to the previous node, which adds the values it receives into its g.
  • loss_vjp does the same for an output node, whose energy is the loss.
  • relax_ moves h and lam by dt seconds; learn_ moves theta.
  • mse and cross_entropy are losses of each sample, for loss_vjp (MSELoss and CrossEntropyLoss hold their batch).

Every g here is a gradient of an energy; the update subtracts it. Gradients are summed over the batch, and the 1 / B (B the number of samples) is applied to theta only (in learn_), so lam holds the credit of each sample. The shapes start with the batch, batch (see activity_spec).

docs.title: vjp
docs.text:
vjp(
    module: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor],
    h_in: Tensor,
    delta: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor],
    params: Sequence[Tensor] = (),
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, list[torch.Tensor]]

Predict mu = module(h_in) and the gradients of the node's energy.

With the activity \(h\) held fixed, the energy \(E = \tfrac12\|h - \mu + \lambda\|^2\) has the gradients

\[ g_{\mathrm{in}} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial h_{\mathrm{in}}} = -J_h^\top \delta,\qquad g_\theta = \frac{\partial E}{\partial \theta} = -J_\theta^\top \delta, \]

where \(\delta = h - \mu + \lambda\) and \(J\) are the Jacobians of module at h_in. Both are summed over the batch. h_in is detached first, so no graph reaches the node that sent it.

PARAMETER DESCRIPTION module

The function f of the node, (*batch, *in) -> (*batch, *out). It must treat the samples independently.

TYPE: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor]

h_in

The activity of the previous node, (*batch, *in).

TYPE: Tensor

delta

Makes \(\delta\) of the node, (*batch, *out), from mu (detached, without gradients), such as lambda mu: h - mu + lam.

TYPE: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor]

params

The parameters to get the gradients of, usually those of module that require gradients.

TYPE: Sequence[Tensor] DEFAULT: ()

RETURNS DESCRIPTION Tensor

(mu, g_in, g_theta): mu ((*batch, *out), detached), g_in

Tensor

((*batch, *in)) and g_theta (one tensor per parameter, in the order of

list[Tensor]

params; a parameter that module does not use gets zeros).

RAISES DESCRIPTION ValueError

delta does not make a tensor of the shape of mu.
