docs.title: 🚨 Errors and Shutdown
docs.text: This page shows what happens when a hook of a node raises, where the host receives the exception, and the timeouts of the host's calls.

docs.title: One node's exception stops everything
docs.text:
Whichever hook of whichever node raises (on_update, on_start, state_dict or any other), the whole run stops:

  1. Mujou logs the node's path, the hook and the traceback to the logger "mujou" at the ERROR level
  2. Each node finishes the hook it is running, stops, and calls its on_exception(), without waiting for the others. The nodes that did not raise are called too
  3. Once every on_exception() has returned, every node's on_stop() is called, the one that raised included
  4. The host gets a NetworkError, a subclass of RuntimeError, whose __cause__ is the first exception. Exceptions of other nodes at about the same time are only logged

Mujou never stops only the node that raised: its neighbors would keep reading its old values and drift away from the equilibrium without anyone noticing.

"""What happens when a node raises.

The whole run stops: every node's ``on_exception``, then its ``on_stop``, is
called, and the host gets a ``NetworkError`` whose ``__cause__`` is the node's
exception. An exception in ``on_start`` comes from ``mujou.run`` itself.
"""

import logging
import sys
from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import NetworkError, Node, Port, TensorSpec

SCALAR = TensorSpec(())

# mujou also logs the node's exception, with its traceback, to the "mujou" logger.
# Show the log on stdout here (without a handler, Python prints it to stderr).
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, format="log: %(message)s")


class Checked(Node):
    """Passes its input on, and raises once it is negative."""

    def __init__(self, fail_on_start: bool = False) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.fail_on_start = fail_on_start
        self.prev = Port(recv=SCALAR)
        self.next = Port(send=SCALAR)

    @override
    def on_start(self) -> None:
        super().on_start()
        if self.fail_on_start:
            raise RuntimeError("cannot start")

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        u = self.prev.recv()
        if u < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"negative input: {u.item()}")
        self.next.send(u)

    @override
    def on_exception(self) -> None:
        super().on_exception()
        print("on_exception: called on every node")

    @override
    def on_stop(self) -> None:
        super().on_stop()
        print("on_stop: called after on_exception")


class Single(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self, fail_on_start: bool = False) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.checked = Checked(fail_on_start)
        self.prev = self.checked.prev


# An exception while the run goes on reaches the host at its next call.
net = Single()
run = mujou.run(net)
run.write({net.prev: torch.tensor(-1.0)})
try:
    run.join(timeout=10.0)  # waits until the run stops (here: by the exception)
except NetworkError as error:
    cause = error.__cause__
    print(f"NetworkError, caused by {type(cause).__name__}: {cause}")
    assert isinstance(cause, ValueError)

# An exception in on_start comes from mujou.run.
try:
    mujou.run(Single(fail_on_start=True))
except NetworkError as error:
    print(f"mujou.run raised NetworkError, caused by {error.__cause__!r}")
    assert isinstance(error.__cause__, RuntimeError)

docs.title: Where the host receives it
docs.text:
The exception happens What raises NetworkError While the run starts (on_start, ...) mujou.run itself, after the ending work (on_exception, on_stop) After the start The next write, read, read_with_time, subscribe (and its iterator), wait_for, state_dict, shutdown or join, or step of a ManualRun

An exception after the start reaches the host at its next call, so a host that only waits does not notice it: wait with run.join(timeout), not with run.timer.sleep. At the end of a with block, the shutdown raises it; if the body of the block raises too, the body's exception goes on and the NetworkError is dropped (the log still has the node's exception).

docs.title: on_exception and on_stop
docs.text:
Hook Called What to write on_exception() When the run ends by an exception, on every node, first The work of an abnormal end, such as a safe stop of the actuators on_stop() Once at every end, normal or not The release of resources such as I/O; not a change of the state
  • on_exception takes no arguments: a node does not learn which exception stopped the run. The host handles the cause, from __cause__
  • To handle an exception within a node, catch it with try in the hook: an exception caught there does not stop the run
  • If on_exception or on_stop raises, the exception is logged, and the ending goes on
  • self.timer does not move in these hooks: see the rules a node keeps

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
The node's exception goes to the logger "mujou" with its traceback; a program that has not configured logging prints it to standard error. Configure Python's logging to send it elsewhere:

# mujou also logs the node's exception, with its traceback, to the "mujou" logger.
# Show the log on stdout here (without a handler, Python prints it to stderr).
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, format="log: %(message)s")

docs.title: The state after an exception
docs.text: The state of a run that ended by an exception is not kept: run.state_dict() raises NetworkError too. Take the state you want to keep while the network runs, regularly during a long run. To run again, build new instances.

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
shutdown, join, subscribe, wait_for and state_dict take a timeout in real seconds; the default math.inf waits as long as it takes.

Call When the time runs out run.shutdown(timeout=...) TimeoutError. The request to stop stands, and the nodes update no more; the ending goes on, and join waits for it run.join(timeout=...) TimeoutError. Nothing changes run.subscribe(port, timeout=...) TimeoutError from the iterator, counting the whole iteration, the body of the loop included. The run keeps running run.wait_for(port, condition, timeout=...) TimeoutError. The run keeps running run.state_dict(timeout=...) TimeoutError, while some node has not paused (each finishes its on_update first). No state is taken, and the run keeps running

A node whose single on_update is long (heavy BP, say) delays every pause for the state.

docs.title: Interpreter exit
docs.text: If the interpreter exits while a run is running, Mujou shuts the run down and waits for every on_stop, once the other non-daemon threads have ended. A thread that iterates over subscribe keeps the exit waiting until its run ends, so end each run yourself, with shutdown or a with block.

docs.title: 🗂️ Groups
docs.text: mujou.run runs one root. To run several networks in one run, put them side by side in a mujou.Group. This page shows how, how paths are named, and when to use separate runs instead.

docs.title: Paths
docs.text:
A node is named by its path: the attribute names from the root, joined with ..

class Stack(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.l1 = Hidden(784, 256)
        self.l2 = Hidden(256, 256)
        self.l1.next.connect(self.l2.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.l1.prev, self.l2.next


class Classifier(mujou.Network):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.body = Stack()  # a network inside a network
        self.head = Head()
        self.body.next.connect(self.head.prev)  # body.next is l2.next itself
        self.prev = self.body.prev  # exposes again a port that the child exposed

The paths of the nodes of Classifier are "body.l1", "body.l2" and "head". A run reads the attributes in the order of assignment, so that is the order of the tree. A node given as the root itself is at "".

Paths are the keys of the state tree, so a network has the same paths however it is run, and renaming an attribute makes a state saved before the rename impossible to restore.

docs.title: Group
docs.text:
# By keyword: two networks connected before they are grouped.
enc, dec = Stage(2.0), Stage(3.0)
enc.next.connect(dec.prev)  # the ports a network exposes, as for nodes
x = torch.tensor([1.0, -1.0])
with mujou.run(Group(enc=enc, dec=dec), inputs={enc.prev: x}) as run:
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes, and how many fit in a given
    # time depends on how the threads get scheduled: follow the output until y
    # arrives (TimeoutError after 5 s).
    # The ports are those of the networks given.
    y, _ = run.wait_for(dec.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 6 * x), timeout=5.0)
    nodes = list(run.state_dict()["nodes"])
print(f"keyword: nodes {nodes}, y = {y}")
assert nodes == ["enc.scale", "dec.scale"]
assert torch.equal(y, 6 * x)

# Two independent networks in one run.
first, second = Stage(2.0), Stage(3.0)
both = Group(first=first, second=second)
with mujou.run(both, inputs={first.prev: x, second.prev: x}) as run:
    y1, _ = run.wait_for(first.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x), timeout=5.0)
    y2, _ = run.wait_for(second.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 3 * x), timeout=5.0)
    nodes = list(run.state_dict()["nodes"])
print(f"side by side: nodes {nodes}, y1 = {y1}, y2 = {y2}")
assert nodes == ["first.scale", "second.scale"]
assert torch.equal(y1, 2 * x) and torch.equal(y2, 3 * x)

Group(enc=a, dec=b) puts each network under its keyword.

Root Path of the node l1 in a a "l1" Group(enc=a, dec=b) "enc.l1" node (a node by itself) "" Group(n=node) "n"

Group connects nothing: connect the networks before or after grouping them, and write and read their ports as they are (enc.prev, dec.next). To restore a state, group the networks with the same keywords as when it was saved.

A node runs once (rules a node keeps), so a network that has run alone cannot join a group: run the networks together from the start, or build new instances.

docs.title: One run or several?
docs.text:
Grouped networks are one run, which shares one timer, one state tree and one ending.

What Grouped in one run In separate runs, each on its own Timer Connecting Possible Not possible: ports of another run cannot be connected Taking the state Pauses every node, and takes one tree at one time One tree per run; taking it pauses only that run Time scale The same for every node May differ per run Exceptions One node's exception ends every network Only the run of the node that raised ends

Use separate runs, each given a mujou.time.Timer(), when one must not pause while the state of the other is taken, when only one should run faster or slower, or when one should keep running if the other fails.

Runs without a timer share the global timer

Runs given no timer all run on mujou.time.global_timer, so taking the state of one pauses the others too. Give each its own Timer to keep them apart (see Time).

docs.title: 🏃 Host I/O
docs.text: The host is the program that runs the network. It talks to a run through the Run that mujou.run returns: it writes inputs, reads outputs and waits. This page covers each of them, and the initial values of the ports.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
The host writes to a Port of the run that receives and is not connected; a node writes the others. Writing to any other port raises ValueError.

t = run.write({net.prev: x, net.teacher: y})  # returns the time of the write
  • A written value stays until the next write: an input is a signal over time, and the nodes read it many times
  • The values of one write switch together. A node never reads the new value of one with the old value of the other, so write values that belong together, such as an input and its target, in one write (or as one DictSpec message)
  • The values are copied: changing the tensor after the write does not reach the network
  • A value of another shape or dtype raises ValueError, and a dict with a missing or an extra key raises TypeError, naming the port

docs.title: Initial values
docs.text:
Way What a reader gets Its time Nothing Zeros None Port(send=..., initial=value) value, until the port first sends None mujou.run(net, inputs={port: value}) value, from the first update The time the run starts run.write({port: value}) value, from the write on What write returned

initial is for a port that a node sends on, and inputs and write are for the ports the host writes. Once mujou.run returns, the nodes start updating, so a write right after it may come after a few updates that read zeros: to show an input from the first update, pass it as inputs.

docs.title: Showing an input for a while
docs.text:
Wait on the run's timer with run.timer.sleep(seconds), which follows the time scale and the pauses of the run:

for x in stream:
    run.write({net.prev: x})
    run.timer.sleep(0.1)  # show x for 0.1 s of the run's time
    y = run.read(net.next)  # the output at the end of the showing time

The output catches up with a change of input after a delay, which the network's dynamics (the time constants of the nodes, the number of stages) decide; choose a showing time long enough. Reading right after write returns the output for an earlier input. When you know the output to expect, wait for it with wait_for instead.

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
Way What it returns Suited for run.read(port) The latest value Reading whenever it suits the host run.read_with_time(port) The latest value and the time it was sent, (value, Timestamp \| None) Telling how new the value is run.subscribe(port) An iterator of (value, Timestamp \| None), each newer than the last Handling each new output run.wait_for(port, until) The first (value, Timestamp \| None) that meets until Waiting until an expected output comes

They read any port of the run that sends, connected or not: reading a connected port observes a value in the middle of the network without changing it. Each returns a new copy on the CPU of what the port last sent with send (its initial value until then, with the time None).

subscribe yields the latest value at once, then waits for each newer one; if the host reads slowly, the values in between are skipped. Its iteration ends when the run ends normally. Leave the loop with break, or pass timeout=:

clock = Clock()  # a node runs by itself, without a network
with mujou.run(clock) as run:
    received: list[tuple[float, float]] = []
    # timeout: give up after 5 s of real time instead of waiting forever.
    for value, t in run.subscribe(clock.next, timeout=5.0):
        if t is None:  # the zeros the port holds until the clock first sends
            continue
        received.append((value.item(), float(t)))
        if len(received) == 20:
            break

wait_for checks the latest value, then each newer one, and returns the first that meets the condition. If the run ends normally first, it raises RuntimeError.

y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, expected), timeout=5.0)

The timeouts are in real seconds, and the default is to wait forever. When one runs out, TimeoutError is raised and the run keeps running (see Errors and Shutdown).

docs.title: Ending
docs.text:
Way What it does with mujou.run(...) as run: Calls shutdown() when the block ends. Use this normally run.shutdown(timeout=...) Asks every node to stop, and waits until every on_stop has returned run.join(timeout=...) Waits until the run ends, without asking it to stop: after another thread called shutdown, or to wait for a node's exception

A run keeps running when the host drops it, until shutdown or the interpreter's exit, so end each run yourself. After a normal end, shutdown does nothing, write raises RuntimeError, and run.state_dict() still takes the last state. If a node raises, the later calls raise NetworkError (see Errors and Shutdown).

docs.title: 🧠 PC-ALM
docs.text: The module mujou.pc learns a PyTorch model split into nodes with PC-ALM (Augmented Lagrangian Predictive Coding, https://pub.sakana.ai/pc-alm/). 5. Learn with PC-ALM builds a chain with pc.Chain and shows it batches with pc.show. This page covers how to choose the time constants, how it differs from BP, the pitfalls, MNIST, and nodes of your own.

docs.title: How it differs from BP
docs.text: Topic BP in plain PyTorch mujou.pc Inference and learning Forward, backward and optimizer.step(), one by one At the same time. Every node updates on its own period, and learns while the input is shown One training step One batch The host shows a batch for a while (S periods). The nodes relax towards the target, then update their weights The target Passed to the loss with the batch Written with the input, and carried in the activity from node to node until the output node Training and test model.train() / model.eval() No modes. A sample whose mask is False is not learned from, so the test batches go through the same running nodes The loss Usually the batch mean The loss of each sample, of the shape of the batch. The output node sums it Where gradients are taken .backward() through the whole model Inside each node only. A node exchanges activities and energy gradients with its neighbors as messages Cost One forward and backward per batch One forward and VJP per node per period, so S of them per batch. On the CPU, MNIST takes about 40 times longer per batch

docs.title: The nodes
docs.text:
Node What it holds Ports pc.Input Its count of writes prev: the host writes a pc.Sample (x, y, mask). next: sends x as the h of a pc.Activity, with y, mask and the time of the write pc.Layer A module, its activity h, the dual lam, its clock prev and next. next sends h as a pc.Activity, with its jumps and the y, mask and time that came with its input pc.Output The last module, the loss, its clock prev. next sends a pc.Prediction (y_hat, y, mask, time) for the host to read

A pc.Activity carries h, jumps, y, mask and time. jumps counts the times the sender's h jumped rather than relaxed: a pc.Input counts the host's writes, and a pc.Layer its moves with a new sample or with a jump of the h it receives, and the jumps that its own weights make when it learns at intervals. A receiver that sees jumps change moves its h with its prediction once, so that the jump does not enter its deviation h - mu.

pc.Chain(*modules, ...) connects Input → Layer → ... → Output, with every period tau.period (tau.h / 4). For other periods or other shapes, build the nodes one by one: give pc.Input the specs x and y and a period, give each pc.Layer and pc.Output the act_spec of the node before it (the spec of the pc.Activity it receives), and connect next to prev along the chain. pc.show shows samples to such a network too, when it exposes the prev of its Input and the next of its Output as its own prev and next.

Put in a node any nn.Module that treats each sample of the batch on its own: one layer, a stack of layers, or a residual block. Dropout and BatchNorm in training mode mix or drop samples, so do not use them; LayerNorm is fine. Initialize the weights when you make the modules: the nodes do not. A parameter with requires_grad=False does not learn.

docs.title: Choosing the time constants
docs.text:
Every rate in mujou.pc is a time in seconds of the run's timer. Choose them in this order.

Value What it sets How to choose it MNIST tau.h How fast each activity h relaxes First. The others follow from it 4 ms The period How often each node updates tau.period (tau.h / 4), the default of Layer and Output and the period of pc.Chain 1 ms tau.lam How fast the dual lam follows 2 * tau.h 8 ms The showing time How long the host shows each batch S periods, with S = 32 32 ms learn_interval When the weights update, counted from the write Longer than half of the showing time, shorter than the showing time, and longer than the round trip of the credit. MNIST uses 3/4 24 ms tau.theta The time constant of the weights (the learning rate is its inverse) The showing time divided by the learning rate per batch 0.32 s max_dt The longest dt one update counts The default, tau.max_dt (min(tau.h / 2, 3 * tau.lam), 2 periods here). A max_dt shorter than the period raises ValueError; so does the default when tau.lam < tau.h / 12 2 ms
  • The learning rate. A weight update moves the weights by (the time since the node last learned) / tau.theta times the mean gradient of the batch. With one update per batch, that time is the showing time, so tau.theta = showing time / lr gives the learning rate lr per batch. The time is the sum of the dt of the updates in between, each capped at max_dt; updates on time have a dt of one period, so it is counted in full
  • The mean gradient. The sum of the per-sample gradients divided by B, the number of samples in the batch (1 without a batch). A sample whose mask is False adds nothing to the sum but still counts in B
  • Why learn_interval is between half and all of the showing time. It is counted from the time the host wrote the input (the time of the activity), not from when a node received it, so the nodes learn at about the same time however deep they are. A node learns learn_interval after each write, and again every learn_interval while the batch is still shown: shorter than half, it learns twice or more per batch. If it is as long as the showing time or longer, the next batch is written first, and the node never learns
  • The round trip of the credit. A node never learns in the update in which it first sees a batch, and the credit needs time to go down the path and back: about 2 * hops * period, with hops the number of connections on the path (3 connections and 6 periods for MNIST, from the Input to the Output). A learn_interval longer than that is recommended. Shorter, the weights learn from a credit that has not settled: in the measurements behind the design, a deep chain whose round trip was 18 periods converged with 16 periods, stayed bounded but off by about 4 times with 4, and diverged with 2 and 1
  • A stream whose input changes at every frame. Pass learn_interval=None: the node then learns in every update, whether or not the input changed, and 1 / tau.theta is the learning rate per second. Good values for streams have not been measured yet
  • Stability. A shorter period relative to tau.h is more stable. In the measurements behind the design, period / tau.h up to 0.5 was stable for ReLU, and period / tau.lam between 0.1 and 0.3 worked best. S = 32 gave the accuracy of BP; shorter showing times have not been verified

docs.title: MNIST
docs.text:
examples/mnist/ learns MNIST with a 784-256-256-10 ReLU network in a pc.Chain, and trains the same network, from the same initial weights on the same batches, by BP. After 3 epochs, PC-ALM reached a test accuracy of 97.60% and BP 97.54% (seed 0).

uv run python examples/mnist/main.py            # 3 epochs, about 2 minutes
uv run python examples/mnist/main.py --epochs 1 --watch

period = args.tau_h / 4  # the period of every node of pc.Chain
shown = args.steps * period  # how long the host shows each batch
# The learning rate of one batch is shown / tau.theta: the nodes learn once
# per batch, for the time since they last learned.
tau = pc.TimeConstants(h=args.tau_h, lam=2 * args.tau_h, theta=shown / args.lr)
net = pc.Chain(
    *modules,
    x=TensorSpec((args.batch, 784)),
    y=TensorSpec((args.batch,), torch.int64),
    batch=args.batch,
    loss=pc.CrossEntropyLoss(args.batch),
    tau=tau,
    learn_interval=0.75 * shown,  # learn once, 3/4 of the way through each batch
)

with mujou.run(net, timer=timer, workers=args.workers) as run:
    for epoch in range(args.epochs):
        right = total = 0
        start = time.perf_counter()
        for i, (x, y, mask) in enumerate(
            batches(data.train_x, data.train_y, args.batch, shuffle(epoch))
        ):
            p = pc.show(run, net, pc.Sample(x=x, y=y, mask=mask), seconds=shown)
            if not torch.isfinite(p["y_hat"]).all():
                raise SystemExit("PC-ALM diverged: lower --time-scale")
            right += correct(p["y_hat"], y, mask)  # before learning from it
            total += int(mask.sum())
            if args.watch and epoch == 0 and i == 100:  # a pause to look
                watch.check(run.state_dict()["nodes"])
        seconds = time.perf_counter() - start
        # Test: the same nodes, with no label to learn from.
        test_right = test_total = 0
        for x, y, mask in batches(data.test_x, data.test_y, args.batch):
            unlabeled = torch.zeros_like(mask)  # keep mask to score with
            p = pc.show(
                run, net, pc.Sample(x=x, y=y, mask=unlabeled), seconds=shown
            )
            test_right += correct(p["y_hat"], y, mask)
            test_total += int(mask.sum())
        results.append(Epoch(right / total, test_right / test_total, seconds))
        print(
            f"PC-ALM epoch {epoch + 1}: prequential {right / total:.2%}, "
            f"test {test_right / test_total:.2%}, {seconds:.1f} s"
        )
  • Prequential accuracy (during training): the first prediction for each batch, which pc.show returns, made before any node has learned from it. It measures how well the model predicts data it has not seen yet
  • Test accuracy: the host shows the test batches with every mask False, so no node learns from them, and keeps the original mask to score with. There is no inference mode to switch to
  • The last batch. data.batches pads the last batch with zeros whose mask is False, so that every batch has the size of the specs. Count only the samples whose original mask is True
  • --watch counts the dt of each node (watch.py), and warns when the updates come later than 1.5 periods (median) or 2 periods (99%)
  • data.py, metrics.py and bp.py do not depend on mujou.pc: the data are plain tensors, and the BP baseline is plain PyTorch

docs.title: The batch
docs.text:
The batch is the shape that every tensor of the messages starts with. Give it as batch to pc.Chain, pc.Input or pc.activity_spec, and start the specs x and y with it. pc.Layer and pc.Output take it from the act_spec they receive.

batch x (784 inputs) y (one class) mask For () (default) (784,) () () One sample at a time, as from a sensor 64 (64, 784) (64,) (64,) 64 samples (8, 4) (8, 4, 784) (8, 4) (8, 4) 4 agents in each of 8 environments, for example
  • The samples must be independent: the module must compute each one on its own, along every dimension of the batch. A dimension that the module mixes, such as the time of a sequence, is a dimension of the sample, not of the batch: 64 sequences of T steps are batch=64 with x of (64, T, 784)
  • A batch of several dimensions learns as the same samples in one dimension: (8, 4) as 32
  • The losses take the batch too: pc.MSELoss(batch) and pc.CrossEntropyLoss(batch). For pc.CrossEntropyLoss, y holds the classes, int64 of the shape of y_hat without its class dimension, or the probabilities of the classes, of the shape of y_hat. The classes are the dimension of y_hat right after the batch, as in nn.CrossEntropyLoss, and the dimensions after them, such as the pixels of an image, are averaged

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Give the batch to the chain and to the loss

The default batch is (), one sample, and the batch is never read from the shapes of the specs. With specs of 64 samples and no batch anywhere, the chain takes the 64 samples as one sample and pc.MSELoss() averages over them: it still runs, but the credit of each sample is 1/64 of what it should be. Pass the same batch to pc.Chain (or pc.Input) and to the loss. If only one of them has it, pc.Output raises an error.

The loss returns the loss of each sample

Pass pc.MSELoss(batch), pc.CrossEntropyLoss(batch), or your own function (y_hat, y) that returns the shape of the batch. A loss that averages over the batch, such as nn.MSELoss(), makes pc.Output raise ValueError. pc.MSELoss averages over every dimension of each sample (all but the batch), as nn.MSELoss does, with no 0.5: the weights follow the gradient of nn.MSELoss() on the batch.

Read predictions from the output node

Predictions come only from the next of pc.Output (net.next of a pc.Chain). A Layer's next sends its activity h with the y, mask and time it passes on, but no prediction. To watch lam of a layer, read it from run.state_dict()["nodes"]["layer0"]["state"]["lam"]; reading the node's attributes while it runs races with its updates.

The activity is zeros until the first sample arrives

Before the host's first write reaches a node, the activity it receives has time 0 and mask all False, so run.read(net.next) returns a prediction with mask all False, and the nodes do not learn. To get the prediction of a batch you wrote, match its time with the time write returned, as pc.show does.

Heavy load can make the network diverge

The nodes exchange messages while each one updates. If a node runs late, its neighbors keep learning from its old messages, and the network can diverge or lose accuracy. MNIST stops when y_hat is not finite; a run that diverges with finite predictions shows only as a falling accuracy. Two causes are known:

  • A time scale that is too fast. MNIST speeds up the run's timer with --time-scale. At 2 instead of 1, the slowest node took most of its period to compute, and 1% of its updates came later than 2 periods. Run one epoch with --watch and take the highest time scale that gives no warning and does not diverge
  • Other processes on the cores. A node that waits for a core lets its neighbors run ahead. On 32 cores at time scale 1, one epoch ran through beside 26 busy processes and diverged beside 32; at 0.5 it ran through beside 32. Run on an otherwise idle machine, or lower the time scale

max_dt does not prevent this. It caps the time each single update counts, and the time beyond it is dropped: from the relaxation and from the next weight update alike.

docs.title: Nodes of your own
docs.text:
mujou.pc.functional holds the computations the nodes are made of: vjp and loss_vjp (the gradients of a node's energy), relax_ (one step of h and lam) and learn_ (the weight update). Use them to write a node that pc.Layer does not cover, such as one with several inputs:

  1. Hold the clock as an attribute: self.clock = pc.LearnClock.of(tau, period=self.period, learn_interval=...), which takes the default max_dt of tau as pc.Layer does. It is in the node's state by itself
  2. In each update, t = self.clock.tick(dt, int(act["time"]), self.timer.now().ns)
  3. When t.new is True or the jumps of the activity differ from those read last, move h with the prediction once: h <- mu + (h - mu_last), with the mu_last of the previous update, and add 1 to the node's own jumps. Keep mu, the jumps read last and your own jumps in the state (register_state for the plain numbers)
  4. Move the activity with pc.functional.relax_(..., t.dt, tau)
  5. Send h as a pc.Activity, with your own jumps and the y, mask and time of the activity you received
  6. When t.learn, learn with pc.functional.learn_(params, g_theta, t.elapsed, tau, batch)

Without step 3, the node follows other dynamics than pc.Layer: a new sample or a jump below enters its deviation h - mu and the credit it sends back. A node that learns at intervals also moves h by the jump of mu that its update of the weights makes, and adds 1 to its jumps; pc.Layer does both one update later, as its docstring describes.

To connect with the nodes of mujou.pc, declare the ports with the act_spec of the node before, or with pc.activity_spec(h, y, batch). The arguments are in the API reference. A rule other than PC that learns across nodes is in Update Rules.

docs.title: 🔌 Ports and Channels
docs.text: A port is a connection point of a node, and connect joins two ports with one channel. This page covers the kinds of ports, their specs, connecting, branching and merging, and what a port holds before anyone sends.

docs.title: The kinds of ports
docs.text:
Kind Peers recv() returns Port At most one if it receives; any number if it only sends The value MultiPort Any number, of one kind A dict[Channel, value], in connect order

Declare ports as attributes of the node in __init__, after super().__init__(); a run reads the attributes of the instance when it starts. A run raises TypeError for a port kept in a list, a tuple or a dict, and the class statement for a port declared as a class attribute: assign each port to an attribute of its own, or use a MultiPort.

Inputs of different roles, such as an input and its teacher signal, or a prediction and an error, go to separate Ports, each with a name that says its role. A MultiPort is for peers of one kind that the node combines the same way.

docs.title: Specs
docs.text:
A port takes the spec of what it sends as send= and of what it receives as recv=, as keyword arguments; leave out the one a one-way port does not use.

self.prev = Port(recv=TensorSpec((32, 784)))  # receives only
self.next = MultiPort(send=TensorSpec((32, 256)), recv=TensorSpec((32, 256)))  # both ways

TensorSpec(shape, dtype) is one tensor; its dtype is torch.float32 unless given, whatever torch.get_default_dtype() is. A value sent must match the spec in shape and dtype: no dtype is converted. The dtypes a spec takes are in TensorSpec.dtypes. A spec also makes values of its shape and dtype, for the state of a node or a test: spec.zeros() and spec.empty() (a dict of them for a DictSpec), and TensorSpec.rand(generator=...).

Values on two ports travel independently: a reader may see a new value on one port with an old one on the other. Send values that belong together, such as an input and its target, as one message: a DictSpec gives a TensorSpec for each key of a TypedDict, the whole dict arrives at once, and type checkers know the type of each key.

class Sample(TypedDict):
    x: torch.Tensor
    y: torch.Tensor


SAMPLE = DictSpec(Sample, x=TensorSpec((32, 4)), y=TensorSpec((32, 2)))

self.next = Port(send=SAMPLE)  # in the sender: self.next.send({"x": x, "y": y})
self.prev = Port(recv=SAMPLE)  # in the receiver: sample = self.prev.recv(); sample["x"]

Type checkers infer the type of a port from its specs. To annotate one (an argument of a helper, say), write Port[S, R] or MultiPort[S, R], where S is the type it sends and R the type it receives; a direction left out is Never, and a type checker rejects a send on a port that sends nothing. A function that takes any spec takes a MessageSpec[T].

from typing import Never

from mujou import MessageSpec, MultiPort, Port


def mean_of(port: MultiPort[Never, torch.Tensor]) -> torch.Tensor:
    return torch.stack(list(port.recv().values())).mean(0)


def sender[T](spec: MessageSpec[T]) -> Port[T]:
    return Port(send=spec)

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
a.next.connect(b.prev) joins two ports and returns the Channel. Nodes and networks have no connect of their own: a node may have several inputs and outputs, and naming the two ports says which path you mean.

  • The spec that each port sends must match the spec the other receives, in both directions; otherwise connect raises TypeError
  • A Port that receives takes one peer: connecting a second raises ValueError. Receive from several with a MultiPort
  • Connecting the same two ports again returns the channel they have. A port may connect to a port of its own node
  • Connections may form cycles: a node may receive from a node it sends to, as the nodes of mujou.pc do on two-way ports
  • A port connects only to ports of nodes in the same run; mujou.run raises ValueError for a peer outside the tree

docs.title: Fan-out and merging
docs.text:
A Port that only sends takes any number of peers, and sends every value to each of them. A MultiPort merges: its recv() returns the latest value of each channel. The value of a peer that has never sent is the initial value of the peer's port.

class Apply(Node):
    """Sends ``fn(x)``."""

    def __init__(self, fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.fn = fn
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)  # only sends: any number of peers

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.fn(self.prev.recv()))


class Sum(Node):
    """Sends the sum of the latest messages of all its peers."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = MultiPort(recv=VECTOR)  # merges any number of peers
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        received = self.prev.recv()  # dict[Channel, torch.Tensor], in connect order
        self.next.send(torch.stack(list(received.values())).sum(dim=0))


class Diamond(mujou.Network):
    """``shift -> (double, square) -> sum``: y = 2 (x + 1) + (x + 1)^2."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.shift = Apply(lambda x: x + 1)
        self.double = Apply(lambda x: 2 * x)
        self.square = Apply(lambda x: x**2)
        self.sum = Sum()
        self.shift.next.connect(self.double.prev)  # one port, two peers
        self.shift.next.connect(self.square.prev)
        self.double.next.connect(self.sum.prev)  # two peers, one MultiPort
        self.square.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.shift.prev, self.sum.next

The receiving node decides how to combine the values: sum them, average them, weight each peer. To treat the peers differently, keep the Channel that connect returned for each, as an attribute of the receiving node (self.sum.from_double = self.double.next.connect(self.sum.prev)), and index with it: self.prev.recv()[self.from_double].

docs.title: Sending to one channel
docs.text:
A MultiPort has two ways to send:

How Where it goes What Run.read returns send(value) The same value to every peer This value send_to(channel, value) Only to the peer at the end of channel Unchanged 
class Split(Node):
    """Sends ``x`` on the channel ``plus`` and ``-x`` on the channel ``minus``."""

    # Channels of self.next, set by the network to the ones connect returned.
    plus: Channel
    minus: Channel

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = MultiPort(send=VECTOR)  # sends to each peer on its own

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        x = self.prev.recv()
        self.next.send_to(self.plus, x)
        self.next.send_to(self.minus, -x)


class Magnitude(mujou.Network):
    """``split -> (relu, relu) -> sum``: y = relu(x) + relu(-x) = |x|."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.split = Split()
        self.pos, self.neg = Apply(torch.relu), Apply(torch.relu)
        self.sum = Sum()
        # Hand split the channels it sends on: the order of connect does not matter.
        self.split.plus = self.split.next.connect(self.pos.prev)
        self.split.minus = self.split.next.connect(self.neg.prev)
        self.pos.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.neg.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.split.prev, self.sum.next

The network hands the node the channels connect returned (self.split.plus = ...). Do not pick channels by their order in self.next.channels instead: swapping two connect calls would swap the destinations without any error. An attribute that holds a Channel is not part of the state.

The host reads with Run.read only what a port sent with send (its initial value until then); it cannot read the values of send_to, nor a port that only receives.

docs.title: Before anyone sends
docs.text:
Until a port first sends, its peers, and the host that reads it, get its initial value: zeros, or the value of initial=, which must match send and is copied when the port is made. Its time is None.

self.next = Port(send=TensorSpec((32, 256)), initial=torch.full((32, 256), 0.5))

recv_with_time() returns the value with the time it was sent (a mujou.time.Timestamp), or None before the first send. Compare it with the time of the value read last to tell a new value from the same one read again. A port that the host writes counts as sent from the inputs= of the run, or from the host's first write: see Host I/O.

docs.title: Exposed ports
docs.text: A network exposes a child's port by assigning it to an attribute of its own (self.prev = self.l1.prev). The attribute is only a reference: the port still belongs to the node, and the outside connects to it as to the node's (x.next.connect(net.prev)). By convention, a network exposes the port of its first node as prev and that of its last as next, so that it connects like a node.

docs.title: 🧵 Threads and Devices
docs.text: This page covers the threads a run computes on, the settings of a node (device, seed, dedicated_thread), CUDA, and the settings of torch that the whole process shares.

docs.title: The arguments of Node
docs.text:
super().__init__ takes these keyword arguments, all optional.

Argument Meaning Default period The time between two updates on average, in seconds of the run's timer 0.01 seed The seed of the node's own random generator self.generator None (different every time) device Where the node computes: "cpu" or a CUDA device "cpu" dedicated_thread Run the node on a thread of its own instead of the run's workers False

The node reads them back as the read-only properties period, generator, device and dedicated_thread.

docs.title: The workers
docs.text:
A run does not start a thread per node. It starts a pool of worker threads, which share the nodes: a worker runs one hook of one node, then takes the next work, the updates due earliest first. With many nodes, the threads stay few, and the OS does not spend its time switching between them.

  • mujou.run(net, workers=n) sets the number of workers. The default is the number of CPUs the process may use (the logical cores, or fewer when the CPU affinity or a quota limits them), or half of it while the GIL is enabled, and never more than the nodes on the workers
  • The hooks of a node never run at the same time, and each sees what the previous one wrote. Which worker runs a node may change from one hook to the next
  • A hook that blocks holds its worker meanwhile, and the other nodes' dt grows (see the rules a node keeps)

While the GIL is enabled (on a build of Python with it, or on the free-threaded build with PYTHON_GIL=1), one thread runs Python code at a time, so the nodes run in parallel only inside torch operations. More workers than half the CPUs mostly contend for the GIL, which is why the default is half there; for nodes that spend most of their time in Python, even fewer are about as fast.

docs.title: A thread of its own
docs.text:
Pass dedicated_thread=True when a node needs a thread of its own:

  • its hooks block, waiting for a device, a socket or a lock: on a worker, the wait would hold the worker
  • it relies on per-thread state set once: its on_start runs on its own thread, so make such settings there
class Camera(Node):
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=1 / 30, dedicated_thread=True)

docs.title: Per-thread settings
docs.text:
On the workers, each hook of a node may run on a different thread, and the thread runs other nodes in between. So whether the next hook sees what a hook set per thread depends on the schedule, and the next node on the same worker may see it too:

  • threading.local, threading.current_thread() and threading.get_ident() may differ from hook to hook
  • Set a per-thread setting of torch, such as torch.autocast or gradient recording, back before the hook returns, by keeping it inside a with in the hook (with torch.no_grad():). A setting left behind leaks into the next node on the worker
  • contextvars do carry over: each node runs its hooks in a contextvars.Context of its own, which starts empty (it does not inherit the host's)

Mujou itself sets only the current CUDA device and stream, before each hook of a CUDA node.

docs.title: Seeds and random numbers
docs.text:
Draw random numbers from the node's own generator, self.generator, made from seed on the node's device. It can be used right after super().__init__(), in __init__ too.

nn.init.normal_(self.model.weight, std=0.1, generator=self.generator)
noise = torch.randn(4, generator=self.generator, device=self.device)

seed reproduces only self.generator. The default initialization of a module such as nn.Linear draws from the global generator that every node shares, so initialize it again from self.generator. Do not call torch.manual_seed in a node: it changes the random numbers of the other nodes too. The state of self.generator is in the node's state, so a resumed run goes on with the same random sequence.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text:
device is the CPU or a CUDA device; any other, such as "mps" or "meta", raises ValueError, and so does CUDA when it is not available. Received messages arrive on the node's device: allocate with device=self.device. "cuda" without an index is fixed to the host's current CUDA device when the node is made.

For a node on CUDA, Mujou:

  • makes the node's device and a CUDA stream of the node's own current in each of its hooks, so every operation of the node goes on its stream
  • waits for the work queued on that stream after each on_update and after the state is restored (the worker waits meanwhile, as in a hook that blocks)
  • waits for it before and after state_dict, on a thread of its own (on the host's thread once the run has ended), so no worker waits for it

So a node writes no synchronization. To synchronize yourself, wait only for your own stream (torch.cuda.current_stream().record_event().synchronize()), never torch.cuda.synchronize(), which waits for the whole device, the other nodes included. A device has a pool of 32 streams, so past 32 CUDA nodes on one device, some nodes share a stream.

Create CUDA tensors and modules in on_start

Tensors and modules made on CUDA in __init__ work: mujou.run synchronizes the host's stream before it starts the nodes. Still, create them in on_start or later. PyTorch's caching allocator ties memory to the stream current when it was allocated, so memory allocated in __init__ stays tied to the host's stream; when the node drops such a tensor, the memory may be reused by the host before the node's work on it has finished. A restore loads the state after on_start, so state made there is restored too.

A node on the CPU does not touch CUDA: on a worker that ran a CUDA node just before, that node's stream is still current, which a CPU node does not use.

The state tree holds CPU copies, also of the nodes on CUDA, and the default load_state_dict copies them back to the node's device. The state of a random generator differs between the CPU and CUDA, though, so a tree saved from nodes on CUDA restores only into nodes on CUDA (on another machine with a GPU too).

docs.title: Settings of the whole process
docs.text:
These settings are shared by the whole process. Do not change them in a node; the host sets them once, before mujou.run:

  • torch.manual_seed and the default random generator
  • torch.set_num_threads, torch.use_deterministic_algorithms and the flags of torch.backends.*
  • operations on a whole device, such as torch.cuda.synchronize() and torch.cuda.empty_cache()

On the CPU, a torch operation uses further threads of its own for each thread that computes. With too many, the nodes compete for the cores and everything slows down, so the host keeps them few:

# The nodes compute on the run's worker threads, and torch adds threads of its
# own for each: keep those few (a setting of the whole process, made by the host).
torch.set_num_threads(1)

Rule of thumb for the number of threads

The number of workers (plus the nodes with dedicated_thread=True) times the n of torch.set_num_threads(n) should not exceed the number of physical cores. With many nodes on small matrices, n = 1 is enough.

docs.title: ⏱️ Time
docs.text: Each run has one time axis, its timer: every node's dt, every message's time and every pause of the run is on it. This page covers the timers, their units, the time scale, pausing, and the timer of a resumed run.

docs.title: The timers
docs.text:
Name What it is mujou.time.global_timer The timer of every run not given one of its own. It starts at 0 when the process first uses it mujou.time.Timer() A timer for a run of its own: mujou.run(net, timer=Timer()). It starts at start (0) with time_scale (1) mujou.time.VirtualTimer() A Timer that moves only when advanced (advance(seconds)); mujou.testing.run uses one mujou.time.ReadOnlyTimer The reading side of a timer: what a node sees as self.timer, with only now() and time_scale() mujou.time.Timestamp A time on a timer

The host controls the time of a run through run.timer: now(), sleep(seconds), pause(), resume(), is_paused(), time_scale() and set_time_scale(scale). A node only reads it, with self.timer.now(), in its hooks.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Unit Used by Seconds of the run's timer dt, period, Timer.sleep, VirtualTimer.advance, pc.show(seconds=), the time constants of mujou.pc Real seconds Every timeout

A timeout is real time so that a stuck run is given up on whatever its time scale and pauses.

docs.title: Timestamp
docs.text:
# A Timestamp: float(t) is seconds, .ns the exact nanoseconds; the difference of
# two is the seconds between them, a float (negative if the first is earlier).
t0, t1 = Timestamp(ns=1_500_000_000), Timestamp(ns=2_000_000_000)
assert float(t0) == 1.5 and t0.ns == 1_500_000_000
assert t1 - t0 == 0.5 and t0 - t1 == -0.5

write, read_with_time, subscribe, wait_for, recv_with_time and now() return Timestamps (or None for a value not sent yet). Compare them with < and the like, and subtract them for the seconds between them. A Timestamp does not record which timer it is on: compare only times of one timer, such as those of one run and its run.timer.now().

t_in = run.write({net.prev: x})
run.timer.sleep(0.1)
y, t_out = run.read_with_time(net.next)
if t_out is not None and t_out >= t_in:  # y was sent after x was written
    print(t_out - t_in)  # seconds from the write until y was sent

docs.title: A timer of a run's own
docs.text:
# A run on a timer of its own, ten times faster than the real time. Pausing this
# timer (or taking this run's state) stops only this run, not the global timer.
timer = Timer(time_scale=10.0)  # starts at 0
clock = Clock()
start_real, start_global = time.perf_counter(), global_timer.now()
with mujou.run(clock, timer=timer) as run:
    run.timer.sleep(2.0)  # 2 s of the run's time: about 0.2 s of real time
    # When the clock updates depends on how the threads get scheduled: wait until
    # it has sent a time from 2 s on. The timeout is in real seconds.
    seen, t = run.wait_for(clock.next, lambda now: now.item() >= 2.0, timeout=5.0)
    assert t is not None  # None only for the zeros before the first send
elapsed_real = time.perf_counter() - start_real
elapsed_global = global_timer.now() - start_global
print(
    f"run's time {float(t):.2f} s, real {elapsed_real:.2f} s, "
    f"global {elapsed_global:.2f} s"
)
# Compare times of the same timer only: a Timestamp does not say which it is on.
assert seen.item() <= float(t)

Give a run a timer of its own to speed up or slow down only that run (for debugging, or for trials faster than real time), or to keep it from pausing with other runs. The time scale is how many seconds of the timer pass per real second: at 10, a real second is 10 seconds of the timer. It is a finite number greater than 0.

The global timer can be scaled too, which changes every run on it:

# The global timer can be scaled too; it then applies to every run on it.
global_timer.set_time_scale(5.0)
start_real = time.perf_counter()
global_timer.sleep(0.5)  # 0.5 s of the global time: about 0.1 s of real time
print(f"slept 0.5 s of global time in {time.perf_counter() - start_real:.2f} s real")
global_timer.set_time_scale(1.0)

docs.title: Pausing the time
docs.text:
timer.pause() stops the time of the timer until timer.resume(); global_timer.pause() stops every run on the global timer. While it is paused:

  • the nodes of every run on the timer do not update, and the first dt after resume does not count the pause. The nodes are not told: on_pause and on_resume run only around taking the state
  • sleep on the timer does not return, and VirtualTimer.advance raises RuntimeError
  • run.state_dict() still works, and gives the state at the time of the pause

Taking the state pauses the run's timer too, apart from your pause: pause is a switch, not a count, and resume does not cut a pause for the state short. is_paused() is true while either one holds the time.

Use it to take the states of several runs on one timer at one time. Taken one after the other, the second state would be of a later time:

# Two runs on the global timer, such as two agents that should be saved together.
# Taken one after the other, the second state would be of a later time; pausing
# the timer they share stops both at one time T.
a, b = Clock(), Clock()
with mujou.run(a) as run_a, mujou.run(b) as run_b:
    global_timer.sleep(0.1)
    global_timer.pause()  # the global time stops at one time T
    try:
        tree_a = run_a.state_dict()  # still works while paused
        tree_b = run_b.state_dict()
    finally:
        global_timer.resume()  # the time goes on from T
t_ns = tree_a["timer"]["time_ns"]
assert tree_b["timer"]["time_ns"] == t_ns  # both are of T
data = pickle.dumps({"a": tree_a, "b": tree_b})  # save them together

Put resume in finally

Then an exception does not leave the time stopped.

A pause is for taking the state and for observing. Do not make pausing part of how a network learns.

docs.title: The timer of a resumed run
docs.text:
A run resumed with mujou.run(net, state=tree) runs on a new Timer that starts at the time and the time scale of the tree, so the global timer and the other runs do not go back:

# A run restored from one of them goes on from T on a timer of its own: the
# global timer does not go back.
saved = pickle.loads(data)
restored = Clock()
with mujou.run(restored, state=saved["a"]) as run:
    assert run.timer is not global_timer
    now, _ = run.wait_for(
        restored.next, lambda now: now.item() > t_ns / 1e9, timeout=5.0
    )
# After the run, its nodes' attributes are the host's to read.
at_save = saved["a"]["nodes"][""]["state"]["elapsed"].item()
print(
    f"run a went on from t = {t_ns / 1e9:.3f} s to {now.item():.3f} s; "
    f"its dt summed to {at_save:.3f} s at the save, {restored.elapsed.item():.3f} s now"
)

Passing timer= with state= raises ValueError, and global_timer.pause() does not pause a resumed run: pause its run.timer. Runs resumed from trees taken at one time therefore no longer share a time axis: their timers drift apart, and pausing one does not pause the others. Runs that must stay on one axis after a resume run as one run (mujou.run(Group(a=a, b=b))), whose single tree resumes onto one timer.

docs.title: Nodes only read the time
docs.text:
A node's self.timer is a ReadOnlyTimer of its run, readable in every hook (on_start included) and nowhere else: reading it in __init__ or from the host raises RuntimeError. It stops at the time the run ends, so on_exception and on_stop see the time stand still.

Only the host moves the time (rules a node keeps). To update at intervals, give the node a period.

docs.title: 🧮 Update Rules
docs.text: An update rule (a learning rule) is what a node writes in on_update(dt). Mujou builds no rule into nodes, ports or the scheduler: each node chooses its own, and the same network can swap them. This page shows how to write a rule that learns across nodes, with feedback alignment as the example; 4. Learn in a Node has backpropagation (BP) inside one node, and PC-ALM the rule of mujou.pc.

docs.title: Within a node, across nodes
docs.text: Inside a node, anything PyTorch computes is allowed, BP included. Across nodes, no computation graph can be joined: a port sends a detached copy. A rule across nodes therefore sends what each node needs as messages: activities forward, errors (or other credits) back, and the targets along with the activities. Each node learns from its own state and its neighbors' messages only.

docs.title: Feedback alignment
docs.text:
examples/feedback_alignment.py learns \(\hat y = W_2 \tanh(W_1 x)\) with two nodes. hidden sends its activity forward, and output sends the error \(e = \hat y - y\) back. BP would give hidden the credit \(W_2^\top e\), but hidden never sees W2: it uses \(B e\) with a fixed random matrix \(B\) of its own, and learns anyway, as \(W_2\) comes to align with \(B^\top\) (Lillicrap et al., 2016).

uv run python examples/feedback_alignment.py

class Hidden(Node):
    """h = tanh(W1 x); learns W1 from the error that comes back through ``B``."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=PERIOD, seed=1)
        g = self.generator
        self.w1 = torch.randn(N_HIDDEN, N_IN, generator=g) / N_IN**0.5
        self.b = torch.randn(N_OUT, N_HIDDEN, generator=g) / N_OUT**0.5  # fixed
        self.clock = pc.LearnClock(
            period=PERIOD, learn_interval=LEARN, max_dt=2 * PERIOD
        )
        self.prev = Port(recv=SAMPLE)  # the host writes it
        self.next = Port(send=ACTIVITY, recv=ERROR)  # two-way

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        sample, t = self.prev.recv_with_time()
        if t is None:  # nothing written yet
            return
        x = sample["x"]
        h = torch.tanh(x @ self.w1.T)
        time = torch.tensor(t.ns)
        self.next.send({"h": h, "y": sample["y"], "time": time})  # relays y
        error = self.next.recv()
        tick = self.clock.tick(dt, t.ns, self.timer.now().ns)
        if tick.learn and int(error["time"]) == t.ns:  # the error of this sample
            delta = (error["e"] @ self.b) * (1 - h**2)  # B e, not W2^T e
            self.w1 -= tick.elapsed / TAU * (delta.T @ x) / BATCH

class Output(Node):
    """y_hat = W2 h; sends the error back, and the loss on each new sample."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=PERIOD, seed=2)
        self.w2 = torch.randn(N_OUT, N_HIDDEN, generator=self.generator) / N_HIDDEN
        self.clock = pc.LearnClock(
            period=PERIOD, learn_interval=LEARN, max_dt=2 * PERIOD
        )
        self.prev = Port(send=ERROR, recv=ACTIVITY)  # two-way
        self.loss = Port(send=TensorSpec(()))

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        act, t = self.prev.recv_with_time()
        if t is None:  # hidden has not sent yet
            return
        h = act["h"]
        e = h @ self.w2.T - act["y"]  # the prediction against its own target
        self.prev.send({"e": e, "time": act["time"]})
        tick = self.clock.tick(dt, int(act["time"]), self.timer.now().ns)
        if tick.new:  # the first update with this sample, before learning from it
            self.loss.send(0.5 * e.pow(2).sum(dim=1).mean())
        if tick.learn:
            self.w2 -= tick.elapsed / TAU * (e.T @ h) / BATCH

The program prints the loss of output on each batch before learning from it, which falls from about 1.5 to about 0.02 in 6 s; with hidden frozen, it stays above 0.15.

docs.title: Two-way ports
docs.text: hidden.next is Port(send=ACTIVITY, recv=ERROR) and output.prev is Port(send=ERROR, recv=ACTIVITY): one connection carries the activity forward and the error back. Connections may form cycles, so the error could as well come back on ports of its own.

docs.title: Relaying the target
docs.text: The activity carries the target y of its sample and the time of the write it came from. Values on two ports travel independently, so a target sent on a port of its own could pair a prediction with the target of another sample. In one message, output always compares a prediction with its own target, and hidden learns only from the error whose time is that of the input it holds. The nodes of mujou.pc carry y, mask and time in their pc.Activity the same way, with jumps, the count of the times the sender's h jumped, which tells the receiver to move its own h with its prediction (PC-ALM).

docs.title: Telling what is new
docs.text: recv() returns the latest value whether or not it is new. A node that learns once from each sample tells a new one by its time: the time recv_with_time() returns, or a time the message carries. Before anyone sends, the time is None (or, for a time in the message, whatever the zeros of the initial value say).

docs.title: pc.LearnClock
docs.text:
Both nodes decide when to learn with a pc.LearnClock, a part of mujou.pc that any rule can use. In each update, tick(dt, time_ns, now_ns) takes the dt, the time the input was written at and the time now, and returns a pc.Tick:

  • new: the input is new (its time is not the one seen last)
  • learn: learn in this update. With learn_interval, that is the first update learn_interval after each write (and every learn_interval while the input stays), but never the update that first sees an input; with learn_interval=None, every update
  • elapsed: the time since the clock last learned, each dt capped at max_dt. Weigh the step with it: \(W \leftarrow W - \frac{\text{elapsed}}{\tau}\,\nabla\) follows the gradient flow \(\tau \dot W = -\nabla\), so how far a node learns depends on time, not on how often it updates
  • dt: the dt capped at max_dt

The clock has state_dict and load_state_dict, so an attribute that holds it is in the node's state by itself. The nodes on a path read the one timer of the run, so they learn at about the same time after each write, however deep they are.

docs.title: 🚀 1. Run a Network
docs.text:
This page runs the smallest program, two nodes that compute \(y = 2x + 1\), and explains it line by line. Then it branches and merges a network.

flowchart LR
    H1["Host"] -->|"writes x"| S["scale (×2)"]
    S --> F["shift (+1)"]
    F -->|"reads y"| H2["Host"]

docs.title: The program
docs.text:
examples/quickstart.py
"""The smallest program: two nodes in a network, running in the background.

The host writes an input, waits until the output arrives, and stops.
"""

from typing import override

import torch

import mujou
from mujou import Network, Node, Port, TensorSpec

VECTOR = TensorSpec((3,))  # every message here is a float32 vector of 3


class Affine(Node):
    """Sends ``a * x + b``, where ``x`` is the latest input."""

    def __init__(self, a: float, b: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.a, self.b = a, b  # settings, not state
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)  # receives from the previous node
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)  # sends to the next node

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.a * self.prev.recv() + self.b)  # recv() never waits




class Pipeline(Network):
    """``x -> scale -> shift ->``: y = 2 x + 1."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = Affine(2.0, 0.0)
        self.shift = Affine(1.0, 1.0)
        self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.scale.prev, self.shift.next  # exposed as its own




net = Pipeline()
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# The nodes run on the run's worker threads until the end of the `with` block.
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x})
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes: wait until y arrives, with
    # the time it was sent (TimeoutError after 5 s of real time).
    y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1), timeout=5.0)
    assert t is not None  # None only for the zeros before the first send

print(f"y = {y} at t = {float(t):.3f} s")

Run it from the root of the repository.

uv run python examples/quickstart.py

It prints one line like this.

y = tensor([3., 5., 7.]) at t = 0.017 s

y is \(2x + 1\) for x = [1, 2, 3]. t is the time at which shift sent y, in seconds of the run's timer. It changes from run to run.

docs.title: A node
docs.text:
class Affine(Node):
    """Sends ``a * x + b``, where ``x`` is the latest input."""

    def __init__(self, a: float, b: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.a, self.b = a, b  # settings, not state
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)  # receives from the previous node
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)  # sends to the next node

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.a * self.prev.recv() + self.b)  # recv() never waits
  • A node is a class that inherits from mujou.Node. As in any subclass, __init__ calls super().__init__() first, and each hook calls the same hook of super() first
  • __init__ declares the node's ports as attributes. Port(recv=VECTOR) receives float32 vectors of 3, and Port(send=VECTOR) sends them. By convention, the port on the side of the previous node is prev and the one on the side of the next node is next
  • a and b are settings: numbers set from the arguments, not state
  • on_update(dt) is one step of the node's work. Mujou calls it again and again, about every 10 ms. recv() returns the latest value the peer sent, without waiting, and send() sends a copy to every peer

docs.title: A network
docs.text:
class Pipeline(Network):
    """``x -> scale -> shift ->``: y = 2 x + 1."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.scale = Affine(2.0, 0.0)
        self.shift = Affine(1.0, 1.0)
        self.scale.next.connect(self.shift.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.scale.prev, self.shift.next  # exposed as its own

A network holds nodes as attributes, connects their ports with connect, and exposes the ports that the outside uses as attributes of its own (self.prev, self.next). connect checks that the spec each port sends matches the spec the other receives, and raises TypeError where it does not.

docs.title: The run
docs.text:
net = Pipeline()
x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# The nodes run on the run's worker threads until the end of the `with` block.
with mujou.run(net) as run:
    run.write({net.prev: x})
    # x takes a few updates to pass through the nodes: wait until y arrives, with
    # the time it was sent (TimeoutError after 5 s of real time).
    y, t = run.wait_for(net.next, lambda y: torch.equal(y, 2 * x + 1), timeout=5.0)
    assert t is not None  # None only for the zeros before the first send

print(f"y = {y} at t = {float(t):.3f} s")
  • mujou.run(net) checks the network, starts every node, and returns a Run once they are running. Each node repeats on_update on the run's worker threads; the host's thread goes on
  • run.write writes x to the unconnected port net.prev. The value stays there until the next write
  • recv() never waits, so shift keeps sending values computed from older inputs (zeros at first) until x has passed through scale. run.wait_for returns the first output that meets the condition, with its time, and raises TimeoutError after 5 seconds of real time
  • Leaving the with block shuts the run down, and an exception of a node reaches the host there at the latest

docs.title: Branching and merging
docs.text:
A Port that only sends takes any number of peers: connect it to several ports, and each gets every value it sends (fan-out). A MultiPort merges: its recv() returns one value per channel, as a dict[Channel, value] in the order of connect, and the node decides how to combine them.

class Apply(Node):
    """Sends ``fn(x)``."""

    def __init__(self, fn: Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.fn = fn
        self.prev = Port(recv=VECTOR)
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)  # only sends: any number of peers

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        self.next.send(self.fn(self.prev.recv()))


class Sum(Node):
    """Sends the sum of the latest messages of all its peers."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.prev = MultiPort(recv=VECTOR)  # merges any number of peers
        self.next = Port(send=VECTOR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        received = self.prev.recv()  # dict[Channel, torch.Tensor], in connect order
        self.next.send(torch.stack(list(received.values())).sum(dim=0))


class Diamond(mujou.Network):
    """``shift -> (double, square) -> sum``: y = 2 (x + 1) + (x + 1)^2."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.shift = Apply(lambda x: x + 1)
        self.double = Apply(lambda x: 2 * x)
        self.square = Apply(lambda x: x**2)
        self.sum = Sum()
        self.shift.next.connect(self.double.prev)  # one port, two peers
        self.shift.next.connect(self.square.prev)
        self.double.next.connect(self.sum.prev)  # two peers, one MultiPort
        self.square.next.connect(self.sum.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.shift.prev, self.sum.next

Diamond computes \(y = 2(x + 1) + (x + 1)^2\): shift sends to both branches, and sum adds what the two send. A Port that receives takes one peer only, because its recv() returns one value; receive from several with a MultiPort. Run it with uv run python examples/branching.py. The same program also sends a different value to each peer, which Ports and Channels explains.

docs.title: 🧩 2. Write a Node
docs.text: This page writes a node whose state follows a differential equation, the leaky integrator, and runs two of them in a row. It covers dt, the state and the period. The rules every node keeps are in How Mujou Works.

docs.title: The node
docs.text:
The node follows its input \(u\) with the time constant \(\tau\): its state \(x\) follows \(\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{u - x}{\tau}\).

class Leaky(Node):
    """Follows its input ``u`` with the time constant ``tau`` (in seconds):

        dx/dt = (u - x) / tau

    ``on_update`` advances ``x`` by ``dt``, the time that passed since the last
    update, with the exact solution for an input held constant over the step:
    ``x`` moves the fraction ``1 - exp(-dt / tau)`` of the way to ``u``. That
    fraction stays below 1 for any ``dt``, so a long ``dt`` (a busy machine) never
    overshoots ``u``, and none of the elapsed time is lost.

    ``period`` is well below ``tau`` by default: a node downstream sees this
    output at most about one period late, a small delay next to ``tau``.
    """

    def __init__(self, tau: float, *, period: float = 0.001) -> None:
        super().__init__(period=period)
        self.tau = tau  # a setting, not state
        self.x = SCALAR.zeros()  # a tensor attribute: in the state by itself
        self.prev = Port(recv=SCALAR)
        self.next = Port(send=SCALAR)

    @override
    def on_update(self, dt: float) -> None:
        super().on_update(dt)
        u = self.prev.recv()
        self.x += (1 - math.exp(-dt / self.tau)) * (u - self.x)  # in place
        self.next.send(self.x)  # a copy: changing x later does not change it

The node writes three things.

  1. In __init__, the settings (tau), the state (x) and the ports (prev, next)
  2. In on_update(dt), it reads the input, moves the state by dt, and sends the result
  3. Nothing else: Mujou calls on_update again and again, so the node has no loop

docs.title: Update in proportion to dt
docs.text:
dt is the time in seconds since this node's previous update, on the run's timer. The first dt counts from the start of the run, once every node's on_start has returned.

Make every update proportional to dt. For \(\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x)\), the simplest update is explicit Euler, x += dt * f(x). A node updates at its own rate, and that rate varies with the load. With updates proportional to dt, every node follows the same dynamics on the same flow of time; a busy machine only makes dt longer. With a fixed step per update instead, a node that loops faster would change faster.

dt is not constant, and it gets longer when the machine is busy. Do not cut it: the time you cut off is lost, and the result drifts from the continuous-time solution. Stay stable for the longest dt that can come instead, in one of two ways.

  • Exact solution: if the system has one, advance the state by dt with it. Leaky moves \(x\) by the fraction 1 - exp(-dt / tau) of its distance to \(u\), which is exact while \(u\) stays constant. The fraction is below 1 for any dt, so \(x\) never overshoots \(u\)
  • Split the step: otherwise, split dt into n steps no longer than a stable length inside one on_update, and update n times in a for loop (4. Learn in a Node does this)

Splitting does not help when the instability comes from the coupling with other nodes, whose messages stay as they were over dt. Such a node may cap the dt it uses, at the cost of the time it drops (the nodes of mujou.pc do, with max_dt).

For noise in a continuous-time update, scale its standard deviation by \(\sqrt{dt}\), not by dt, so that the result does not depend on how often the node updates.

docs.title: The state
docs.text:
self.x is a tensor attribute, so it is in the node's state by itself: run.state_dict() takes it, and a restore loads it back (see 6. Save and Resume). Create the state in __init__, and update it in place in on_update (+=, copy_ and the like).

Assigning a new tensor to the attribute raises no error, and the new tensor is the state from then on. What breaks is any other reference to the first tensor, from another attribute or an optimizer: it still points at the old one. A restore also writes in place into the tensor the node holds.

self.tau is a number set from an argument: a setting, not state. A node restored with another tau keeps its own. A plain value that changes while the node runs, such as a counter, joins the state with register_state (4. Learn in a Node does this).

The node sends self.x, and changes it in place afterwards. That is fine: send copies the value.

docs.title: The period
docs.text:
A node updates once every period seconds on average, 0.01 s by default. The time on_update takes counts toward the period, and a node that falls behind does not update several times in a row to catch up. Leaky takes a period of 1 ms by default, well below tau: a node downstream sees the output at most about one period late, a small delay next to tau.

Even with a period, dt is not exactly period: it is the time that actually passed, longer after a delay and shorter after that. Keep updating in proportion to dt.

In a chain fed by a node with a period (a sensor, say), the nodes after it read the same input until the next one arrives. Give them a period no longer than the period of their input.

period=0.0 uses up a CPU core

period=0.0 calls the next on_update as soon as any time has passed. Such a node keeps a CPU core busy, takes time from the other nodes and makes their dt irregular. Pass it only to a node that really must not wait.

docs.title: Two in a row
docs.text:
class LeakyChain(Network):
    """``u -> a -> b ->``: two leaky integrators with the time constant ``tau``."""

    def __init__(self, tau: float) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.a = Leaky(tau)
        self.b = Leaky(tau)
        self.a.next.connect(self.b.prev)
        self.prev, self.next = self.a.prev, self.b.next

leaky.py steps the input of the chain from 0 to 1, and compares the outputs with the exact solution at the time each was sent:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    tau = 0.05
    net = LeakyChain(tau)
    with mujou.run(net) as run:
        # Step the input from 0 to 1 (write returns the time of the step), then
        # watch both integrators rise on the run's timer.
        start = run.write({net.prev: torch.tensor(1.0, dtype=torch.float64)})
        for _ in range(4):
            run.timer.sleep(tau / 2)
            a, t_a = run.read_with_time(net.a.next)
            b, t_b = run.read_with_time(net.b.next)
            # Each output against the exact one at the time it was sent. On a busy
            # machine a node may not have sent since the step: its time is then
            # earlier than start, and the difference is negative (None, before
            # its first send, counts as long before the step).
            exact_a, _ = step_response(-math.inf if t_a is None else t_a - start, tau)
            _, exact_b = step_response(-math.inf if t_b is None else t_b - start, tau)
            print(
                f"a = {a.item():.3f} (exact {exact_a:.3f}), "
                f"b = {b.item():.3f} (exact {exact_b:.3f})"
            )
        # Hold the input for 10 time constants: both reach the equilibrium x = u.
        run.timer.sleep(10 * tau)
        b = run.read(net.next)
    print(f"after {10 * tau:.1f} s more: b = {b.item():.4f}")

uv run python examples/leaky.py

run.write returns the time of the step, and run.read_with_time the time of each output: their difference is the time since the step, on the run's timer, however the nodes got scheduled.
